summary: Research the ADF plus SAP Integration Suite middleware estate at senior level, refute it, and extract the silent-failure scenarios

draft.area: ADF plus SAP ingestion path (SAP extraction options, self-hosted integration runtime, mapping data flows versus copy activity, triggers and CDC delta state)
corrections_to_my_facts: MATERIAL OMISSION, and it changes the shape of this chapter. Microsoft Learn now carries an Important banner at the top of the SAP CDC architecture page: 'A recent update of SAP Note 3255746 announces a security patch that blocks incoming calls to the ODP RFC API from third-party clients including Azure Data Factory's SAP CDC connector.' It points at SAP Notes 3255746 and 3439624 and lists replacements (Mirroring for SAP Datasphere in Fabric, SAP Business Data Cloud Connect for Microsoft Fabric, a Copy Job in Fabric for SAP with a Microsoft ABAP Add-on that does not use the ODP RFC API, and partner solutions with Open Mirroring). A booklet written in August 2026 that presents SAP CDC over ODP as the default senior choice is out of date on the day it ships. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-introduction-architecture

Everything you verified about ADF Git is confirmed verbatim against https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control (page updated 2026-07-29). Exact wording: 'The main branch isn't representative of what's deployed in the Data Factory service. The main branch must be published manually to the Data Factory service.' And: 'Changes made via PowerShell or an SDK are published directly to the Data Factory service and aren't entered into Git.' And on Key Vault: 'Any changes to Linked Services containing secrets such as passwords are published immediately to the Azure Data Factory service.' No correction needed.

One nuance to add to your publish_config.json fact: 'Data Factory only reads the publish_config.json file when it loads the factory. If you already have the factory loaded in the portal, refresh the browser to make your changes take effect.' Also, the docs now describe a repo setting to disable the Publish button in ADF Studio, which is the intended posture when an automated release pipeline owns publishing. Both are on the same source-control page.

Your Checkpoint Key fact is right but incomplete in a way that bites: 'The Checkpoint Key property is not shown if the Run mode within the SAP CDC source is set to Full on every run, because in this case no change data capture process is established.' So a data flow silently loses its checkpoint identity when someone flips run mode to full, and gets a fresh one when they flip back. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-sap-change-data-capture

Your ODQMON fact is right, and the exact limitation wording is worth quoting because it is short: 'You can't reset or delete ODQ subscriptions in Data Factory (use transaction ODQMON in the connected SAP system for this purpose).' The second bullet in the same list is 'You can't use SAP hierarchies with the solution.' Both are under Current limitations on the connector page.

Add the ODP context vocabulary to your SAP CDC fact, because it is what a senior person actually parameterises: ABAP_CDS, BW, HANA, SAPI, and SLT~<Queue Alias> (the queue alias comes from Administration Data in transaction LTRC). ODP_SELF and RANDOM exist but are for SAP's own technical validation. Run mode parameter values are fullAndIncrementalLoad, fullLoad, incrementalLoad. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics

Refinement on SLT: SLT is not required for the SAP CDC connector generally. Microsoft states 'SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server (SLT) is only required if you want to replicate data from SAP tables with the SAP CDC connector. All other sources work out-of-the-box without SLT.' SLT as proxy needs NetWeaver 7.4 SPS 04 or later plus the DMIS 2011 SP 05 add-on. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-prerequisites-configuration

SAP Datasphere naming, since you asked what it was called before: SAP's own learning content says 'Originally, SAP Datasphere began as SAP Data Warehouse Cloud. SAP decided to combine the features of SAP Data Intelligence with SAP Data Warehouse Cloud to create SAP Datasphere.' Note the help.sap.com documentation pages render client side and returned empty bodies to a plain fetch, so this is sourced from learning.sap.com plus the Microsoft Fabric mirroring page, not from the SAP Help Portal HTML. Flagging that as a sourcing weakness rather than presenting it as SAP Help Portal verified.

Your framing treats the ADLS Gen2 staging area as an implementation detail. Microsoft is more prescriptive: 'The staging folder should be considered an internal storage of the SAP CDC connector... We therefore recommend not to use the staging folder for other purposes, e.g. as a source for other copy activities or mapping data flows.' Teams that point a Databricks Auto Loader at that folder are building on a format Microsoft reserves the right to change.

products.name: SAP CDC connector (mapping data flow source)
products.vendor: Microsoft (Azure Data Factory / Azure Synapse Analytics)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Delta extraction from any ODP capable SAP system without watermark columns, and the only ADF connector that sees deletes. Mapping data flow only, no copy activity, no lookup. Requires an ADLS Gen2 staging linked service that cannot use a self-hosted integration runtime, and a Checkpoint Key that must be unique per source. As of the current Learn page it is the connector SAP Note 3255746 is designed to block, so senior use in 2026 is mostly exit planning: inventory subscriptions, prove the alternative, decommission cleanly in ODQMON.

products.name: Self-hosted integration runtime (SHIR)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The only way ADF reaches an on-premises or network isolated SAP system. Senior concerns are node topology (up to four nodes, credentials encrypted with DPAPI and synced node to node), concurrent job ceiling per node, the one-year version expiry that turns a node offline, and the fact that a data flow staging store cannot route through it. Sizing anchor from Microsoft: recommended minimum 2 GHz, 4 cores, 8 GB RAM, 80 GB disk; an internal Microsoft test reached above 12 MB/s with parallel SAP extractions on a 16 core SHIR host.

products.name: SAP Table connector
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Copy activity read of transparent, pooled and clustered tables and views over RFC, via /SAPDS/RFC_READ_TABLE2 or a customRfcReadTableFunctionModule. No delta semantics at all, so the engineer owns the watermark and cannot see deletes. Chosen for reference and configuration tables, for one-off reconciliation pulls, and increasingly as the non-ODP fallback. Partitioning is explicit: partitionOption of PartitionOnInt, PartitionOnCalendarYear, PartitionOnCalendarMonth, PartitionOnCalendarDate or PartitionOntime, with maxPartitionsNumber recommended as a multiple of parallelCopies.

products.name: SAP BW Open Hub connector
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Reads an Open Hub Destination local table in SAP BW after a DTP has written into it, using request IDs as the delta boundary via excludeLastRequest (default true) and baseRequestId. Senior value is that the SAP side owns the delta and ADF only advances a request pointer. Two hard rules: the OHD must be type Database Table with Technical Key checked, and you must not create more than one DTP per OHD, so full and delta from the same InfoProvider need two OHDs. Does not support SAP BW/4HANA.

products.name: SAP HANA connector
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: SQL level read of HANA tables and information models (analytic and calculation views) through the HANA ODBC driver on a SHIR. Used when the semantic layer lives in HANA views and the ABAP layer would only get in the way, and for heavy parallel full loads using PhysicalPartitionsOfTable or SapHanaDynamicRange with the ?AdfHanaDynamicRangePartitionCondition placeholder. Source only: writing back to HANA means the generic ODBC connector, a different linked service type that cannot be reused.

products.name: SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server (SLT)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Trigger based CDC on SAP application tables, used as an ODP proxy so that tables (not just extractors and CDS views) can feed the operational delta queue. Configured in transaction LTRC with RFC Connection, scenario Operational Data Provisioning (ODP), and a Queue Alias that becomes the ADF ODP context SLT~<alias>. Needs NetWeaver 7.4 SPS 04 or later and the DMIS 2011 SP 05 add-on. Note that the Matillion tech note reads SAP Note 3255746 as also prohibiting SLT for third-party export, which is the question to put to your SAP licensing contact.

products.name: Operational Data Provisioning framework and transaction ODQMON
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The provider and subscriber machinery that the whole CDC story rests on. ODQMON is where a senior engineer actually works: filter by the linked service Subscriber name, open a queue by table name (for example EKKO), inspect subscriptions and the request list that maps one to one onto data flow runs, tick Calculate Data Volume to compare SAP side row counts against ADF row counts, and delete subscriptions that are no longer needed so SAP stops retaining unconsumed packages. Validation harness is program RODPS_REPL_TEST.

products.name: SAP Connector for Microsoft .NET (SAP NCo 3.0), 64 bit
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The RFC client library that every RFC based ADF SAP connector loads. Must be installed on each SHIR node with Install Assemblies to GAC selected. It is the classic cause of a node that registers fine and then fails only on SAP activities, and it is why SHIR nodes are not interchangeable commodity VMs: build them from an image, not by hand.

products.name: SAP Datasphere (formerly SAP Data Warehouse Cloud), with Premium Outbound Integration
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: SAP's sanctioned egress path now that ODP RFC is being closed. A Datasphere replication flow extracts the initial snapshot plus changed records from S/4HANA, ECC, BW, BW/4HANA or Datasphere itself and lands them in an ADLS Gen2 container, which downstream tooling then consumes. Premium Outbound Integration is a separately priced volume based entitlement, so it converts an engineering problem into a licensing negotiation. Renamed from SAP Data Warehouse Cloud when SAP folded in SAP Data Intelligence capability.

products.name: Tumbling window trigger
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The only ADF trigger with state, retry and dependency semantics, and the one Microsoft explicitly prescribes for SAP CDC: create it with Max concurrency 1 and add a self dependency so a run never overlaps its predecessor. One to one with a single pipeline. maxConcurrency is 1 to 50, minimum window 5 minutes, frequency and interval are immutable after publish, dependencies cap at five, and a window waits on dependencies for seven days before failing.

products.name: Mapping data flows on Azure Integration Runtime (Spark)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Mandatory for SAP CDC because the ODP change feed carries technical attributes such as ODQ_CHANGEMODE and can contain several changes to the same key in one extract. Senior tuning levers: compute size (4/4 small through 256/16 cores), Time to live to avoid a 3 to 5 minute cold Spark start on sequential flows (unavailable on the auto resolve IR), shuffle partitions from 50 to 2000 at roughly 1.5 GB per partition, and logging level dropped from Verbose to Basic or None in production.

products.name: Fabric alternatives to the ODP path: Mirroring for SAP via SAP Datasphere, SAP Business Data Cloud Connect for Microsoft Fabric, Copy Job for SAP with ABAP Add-on
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The named exits from the ODP RFC block on Microsoft's own page. Mirroring is generally available and works Datasphere replication flow to ADLS Gen2 to OneLake Delta. BDC Connect was announced at Ignite 2025 with SAP terms that restrict downstream use of the shared data, which is a real constraint on a Snowflake plus Databricks estate. The Copy Job with a Microsoft supplied ABAP Add-on is stated as publicly available at Microsoft Build 2026 and deliberately does not use the ODP RFC API. All three land in Fabric, not in ADF, which is the strategic point.

senior_scenarios.title: Rebuilding a delta subscription on a high volume extractor without losing rows or taking a multi day outage
senior_scenarios.narrative:
A finance extractor over ABAP_CDS with roughly 1.4 billion rows has been running fullAndIncrementalLoad on a 15 minute tumbling window for two years. The Checkpoint Key was reused across a parameterised data flow that also serves three other sources, and the states have collided. You cannot repair a Checkpoint Key: changing it starts a new change data capture process, and fullAndIncrementalLoad would re-request a complete snapshot from SAP, which on this object is a multi day extraction the SAP basis team will not authorise during quarter close.

The move a senior person makes is to decouple the two halves of the run mode. First, publish a second data flow in incrementalLoad mode with the new unique Checkpoint Key and let it run once. That creates the ODP delta subscription without pulling a snapshot, so from that instant every change is accumulating in the operational delta queue. Only then start a separate fullLoad data flow, partitioned in the Optimize tab with Source partition conditions on GJAHR so the fiscal year ranges extract in parallel, writing to a landing zone. Full mode establishes no CDC process, so it cannot disturb the new subscription.

Merge by the declared Key columns, newest wins, with the full snapshot as the base and everything the incremental subscription accumulated replayed on top. Confirm in ODQMON, by Subscriber name, that exactly one live subscription remains and the old one is deleted so SAP stops retaining its unconsumed packages.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The obvious move (reset the checkpoint and let fullAndIncrementalLoad re-initialise) is the one that costs days of SAP load and a reporting gap. The safe move requires knowing that incrementalLoad opens a subscription without a snapshot, that fullLoad establishes no CDC process at all and therefore cannot corrupt one, and that ODP retains changes from the moment the subscription exists rather than from the moment the snapshot completes. Nothing in the ADF user interface tells you the ordering matters. Partition conditions are also unchecked: Microsoft states plainly that overlapping filter conditions are the user's responsibility, so a badly split GJAHR range silently double counts.

senior_scenarios.title: An ODP extractor whose deltas silently stopped after an SAP transport, while every pipeline stayed green
senior_scenarios.narrative:
A transport goes into production on a Tuesday night. From Wednesday the sales pipeline still runs every 15 minutes, every tumbling window succeeds, the data flow reports success, and Power BI keeps refreshing. Row counts simply plateau. Nobody is paged, because ADF has nothing to fail on: an empty delta is a valid delta.

The diagnosis lives on the SAP side, not in ADF. In ODQMON you filter by the Subscriber name configured on the SAP CDC linked service, open the queue, and compare the subscription's request list against the data flow run history. If the requests stop appearing, ADF is polling a queue nobody is filling: the transport re-imported the DataSource and dropped its release for ODP extraction (SAP Note 2232584), or it changed the CDS view so the extraction annotations no longer populate the ODQ (SAP Note 3038236). If the requests are there with the expected counts, the loss is downstream and ADF owns it.

The trap during triage is the developer who reproduces it in debug mode and reports that it works. Debug runs use a different subscriber process value from triggered runs, so they open their own subscription in SAP, and that subscriber process only lives as long as the browser session. A debug run proves nothing about the production subscription. Microsoft says it directly: to test stability over days, publish and use triggered runs.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The failure is on the far side of an organisational boundary and produces no error anywhere in Azure. Senior instinct has to be to reach for an SAP transaction, not an ADF monitor, and then to compare two independent row counts across systems rather than trusting either. The debug versus triggered subscriber process distinction is buried in an advanced topics page and is exactly the sort of detail that turns a two hour incident into a two week one. Layered on top: from June 2026, an SAP support package rather than a transport can produce the same silent stop, because SAP Note 3255746 blocks the ODP RFC calls outright.

senior_scenarios.title: Getting off ODP RFC before SAP Note 3255746 takes the estate down, with the warehouse split across Snowflake and Databricks
senior_scenarios.narrative:
Microsoft's own SAP CDC architecture page now opens with a warning that a security patch announced in SAP Note 3255746 blocks incoming calls to the ODP RFC API from third-party clients including the ADF SAP CDC connector, and points at Notes 3255746 and 3439624. Secondary reporting puts technical enforcement at 9 June 2026 with a time limited opt-out (SAP Note 3731818) expiring around December 2026. Treat the dates as needing confirmation from your own SAP contacts; treat the direction as settled.

The senior work is triage, not tooling. Inventory every Checkpoint Key and every ODQMON subscription and map each to a business consumer, because a good share will turn out to be feeding a dashboard nobody opens. Split what remains three ways. Objects with no true delta need (configuration, master data, small dimensions) move to the SAP Table connector with explicit partitioning and an owned watermark, since that path is plain RFC table reads and is not ODP. Objects that already flow through BW move to Open Hub, where SAP's DTP owns the delta and ADF only advances a request ID. Everything genuinely transactional and high volume goes to a sanctioned path: SAP Datasphere replication flows landing in ADLS Gen2, then into Snowflake or Databricks, with Premium Outbound Integration priced by volume.

The uncomfortable part is that Microsoft's named replacements all land in Fabric, and this estate is Snowflake plus Databricks with Power BI on top.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The forcing function is a vendor licensing and security decision, not an engineering one, so no amount of ADF skill avoids it. The migration must be sequenced against a hard cutover date, on objects whose delta history cannot be reconstructed once a subscription is gone, while an SAP basis team applies support packages on its own calendar. Premium Outbound Integration turns a technical choice into a commercial one, and the Fabric shaped alternatives conflict with a warehouse strategy already committed to Snowflake and Databricks. Deciding what to let die is the highest value work here, and it is the part no tool does for you.

silent_failures.failure: Two SAP CDC sources share one Checkpoint Key, so one source's change data capture state overwrites the other's. Both pipelines keep succeeding and both keep returning plausible looking deltas.
silent_failures.why_invisible: There is no uniqueness constraint and no warning. Microsoft only says it is 'important to use a unique Checkpoint Key for each source. Otherwise status information of one source will be overwritten by another source.' The symptom is missing rows for one object, not an error, and the two data flows may be owned by different people. It gets worse with metadata driven design, which is precisely the pattern Microsoft recommends: one parameterised data flow serving hundreds of sources multiplies the blast radius. Related trap: the Checkpoint Key property is hidden entirely when Run mode is Full on every run, so it can silently vanish and reappear as a fresh key when someone toggles run mode.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A reconciliation, not a monitor. For each object, compare Rows copied in the ADF data flow monitor against the request row counts under the matching subscription in ODQMON, filtered by the linked service Subscriber name, over the same window. Independently, assert uniqueness as a build gate: extract every checkpointKey value from the published pipeline JSON in the collaboration branch and fail the pull request if the sorted list has duplicates. That is a grep that must return empty, and it runs in CI rather than in someone's head.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-sap-change-data-capture (Transform data with the SAP CDC connector, Checkpoint Key) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics (Parameterizing the Checkpoint Key)

silent_failures.failure: A developer validates a CDC change in debug mode, sees correct data, and ships. The published triggered pipeline behaves differently because it uses a different ODP subscription.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Debug and triggered runs use different subscriber process values, so they create separate change data capture processes inside SAP. The debug subscriber process also has a lifetime limited to the browser user interface session. A debug run therefore tests a subscription that will not exist tomorrow and that has none of production's accumulated state. The output looks identical to a correct production run, which is exactly why it is trusted. The same mechanism makes incident triage misleading: reproducing in debug 'proves' the pipeline is healthy while the production subscription is dead.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A rehearsal, in the literal sense Microsoft prescribes: 'To test stability of a change data capture process with SAP CDC over a longer period of time (say, multiple days), data flow and pipeline need to be published, and triggered runs need to be executed.' Make multi day triggered soak on a non production factory a merge requirement for any CDC change, and check in ODQMON that the subscription under the production subscriber process advanced across that period. A single green debug run is not evidence and should not be accepted as one in review.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics (Debugging)

silent_failures.failure: An SAP BW Open Hub feed is permanently one DTP request behind, or double counts, because excludeLastRequest defaults to true and someone created a second DTP writing into the same Open Hub Destination.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The default is deliberate and correct: excluding the last request is what stops ADF reading a table the DTP is still writing into. But it means the warehouse is structurally never fully current, which reads as a data quality complaint about staleness rather than a configuration fact. The multiple DTP failure is worse: request IDs from different DTPs interleave in one Open Hub table and the baseRequestId pointer no longer means what the pipeline assumes, so rows are skipped or replayed with no error. Microsoft states the rule flatly: 'it's not allowed to have request IDs from different DTPs in the same Open Hub table... you must not create more than one DTP for each Open Hub Destination.'
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A second derivation plus a row count. Reconcile the target table against the source InfoProvider for a closed period, not against the Open Hub table, since the Open Hub table shares the same defect. Separately, run a control query over the Open Hub table grouping by DTP request ID to prove exactly one DTP has ever written to it, and assert that the max requestId copied in the last run matches the stored watermark. Also check the DTP's SAP HANA Execution flag: Microsoft documents that leaving it on caps the copy at the first batch, roughly one million rows, with no failure.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-sap-business-warehouse-open-hub (Delta extraction flow; Troubleshooting tips)

silent_failures.failure: Rows calculated is lower than Rows copied in the data flow monitor, and someone 'fixes' the phantom data loss.
silent_failures.why_invisible: It looks exactly like rows being dropped in transit, and the numbers are right there side by side in the monitor. It is in fact correct behaviour: the ODP change feed can contain several changes to the same key in one extract, and the data flow deduplicates on the declared Key columns so only the most recent record continues downstream. The real failure mode is the inverse and it is silent: if Key columns are declared wrongly (for example VBELN without POSNR on VBAP, or omitting MANDT in a multi client system) the deduplication collapses distinct business rows into one and the counts still look reasonable.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A second derivation of the key. Prove uniqueness at source before trusting the sink: run a count versus distinct count on the declared key columns over a full snapshot and require they match exactly. Then reconcile a closed period end to end, source system total against warehouse total, rather than eyeballing Rows copied against Rows calculated. Treat any divergence between count and distinct count as a blocking defect in the Key columns definition, not as a data quality observation.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-management (Monitor SAP CDC data flows) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics (Key columns)

silent_failures.failure: A self-hosted integration runtime node passes its one year version expiry, or a high availability pair drifts out of credential sync, and SAP extraction degrades rather than stopping.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Microsoft states that 'Each version of self-hosted integration runtime expires in one year' and that on expiry the node 'will display an offline status and no longer work properly.' In a multi node gateway the surviving nodes absorb the load, so throughput drops and timeouts appear intermittently while the logical integration runtime still reports healthy enough to run. The credential case is nastier: if the dispatcher node holds credentials that never synced to the workers, everything works until a failover, and then activities fail on credential access for reasons that look like an SAP authorisation problem. Auto update also masks version drift, since Microsoft pushes a stable version from the preceding three months rather than the latest.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A row count over your own estate, run on a schedule rather than after an incident. Microsoft publishes a PowerShell and Azure CLI script on the auto update page that enumerates every factory and every self-hosted integration runtime and flags expired or expiring versions; run it monthly and require the expiring list to be empty. For high availability, assert the credential sync version is identical across nodes before declaring a node healthy, and prefer Azure Key Vault backed linked services so credentials are not stored on the nodes at all. Verify failover by actually failing one node over in a maintenance window.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/self-hosted-integration-runtime-auto-update (Self-hosted Integration Runtime Expire Notification) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/self-hosted-integration-runtime-troubleshoot-guide (Credential sync issue causes credential loss from HA)

silent_failures.failure: The tumbling window trigger runs CDC windows concurrently, or a backfill fires hundreds of windows at once, and deltas are applied out of order.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The trigger and every pipeline run report success. maxConcurrency accepts 1 to 50 and defaults are easy to leave wrong, and if startTime is in the past ADF generates M = (CurrentTime - TriggerStartTime) / TumblingWindowSize backfill runs in parallel, honouring concurrency, before any future run. Each window pulls whatever is currently in the operational delta queue, so two windows running at once against one subscription do not partition the change stream cleanly, they race it. The sink ends up internally consistent looking and wrong. Microsoft's guidance for SAP CDC is explicit and is the thing people skip: Max concurrency 1, plus a self dependency so a run waits for its predecessor.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A reconciliation against an ordering invariant, plus a configuration assertion. Assert in CI that every trigger referencing a SAP CDC pipeline has maxConcurrency of 1 and a SelfDependencyTumblingWindowTriggerReference with a negative offset; that is a JSON check that must return empty on violation. Then prove ordering empirically: pick a handful of business keys that changed several times inside one window and confirm the sink holds the last state, not an earlier one. Before enabling any trigger whose startTime is in the past, compute M by hand and, per Microsoft's own recommendation, do an initial historical load instead of letting the trigger backfill a long period.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/how-to-create-tumbling-window-trigger (Execution order of windows in a backfill scenario; maxConcurrency) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-management (Run an SAP data replication pipeline on a recurring schedule)

silent_failures.failure: A non Key Vault linked service or integration runtime JSON is published to the live service the moment it is created, so Git and the running factory disagree and the publish branch goes stale.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The user interface accepts everything and the collaboration branch looks like the truth. Microsoft lists the exact scenarios that produce a stale publish branch: a user deletes a non Key Vault linked service in a feature branch that is never merged; a user modifies the factory with the SDK or PowerShell; a user uploads a non Key Vault linked service or integration runtime JSON manually and references it from a dataset, which the user interface permits because it exists in Git and which is then rejected at publish time because it does not exist in the service. Every one of these produces a factory whose deployed state differs from main with no failing build to show for it.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A reconciliation between Git and the live service, run as a scheduled job rather than at release time. Export the live factory definition through the REST API or PowerShell and diff it against the collaboration branch; any non empty diff outside of expected Key Vault indirection is a finding. Two documented remedies exist and they point in opposite directions, so choose deliberately and record which is authoritative for your estate: Overwrite live mode treats the repository as source of truth (collaboration branch to live mode), while disconnecting and reconnecting Git treats live mode as source of truth (live mode to collaboration branch). Also disable the Publish button in ADF Studio once an automated release pipeline owns publishing.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control (Stale publish branch; Using passwords from Azure Key Vault; Editing repo settings)

checked.area: ADF plus SAP ingestion path (SAP extraction options, self-hosted integration runtime, mapping data flows versus copy activity, triggers and CDC delta state), adversarially re-verified against Microsoft Learn and third party SAP Note reporting, August 2026
corrections_to_my_facts: SCENARIO 1 REFUTES ITS OWN PREMISE. The narrative rejects the obvious repair because 'fullAndIncrementalLoad would re-request a complete snapshot from SAP, which on this object is a multi day extraction the SAP basis team will not authorise during quarter close', and then prescribes a separate fullLoad data flow over the same 1.4 billion rows. The snapshot cost is not avoided. Every mechanic in the scenario is doc confirmed (incrementalLoad 'creates an ODP delta subscription without returning an initial full data snapshot in the first run'; fullLoad 'extracts a current full data snapshot without initiating a change data capture process'; source partitioning is offered only when Run mode is Full on every run or Full on the first run then incremental), but the stated benefit is wrong. The real benefit is that the delta subscription starts accumulating from the moment it is opened, so the snapshot can be deferred past quarter close and parallelised without a delta gap. Ship the corrected rationale, not the original one. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-sap-change-data-capture and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics

SCENARIO 2 CONTAINS A MECHANIC DESCRIBED BACKWARDS. Its why_hard says 'from June 2026, an SAP support package rather than a transport can produce the same silent stop, because SAP Note 3255746 blocks the ODP RFC calls outright.' A block on incoming ODP RFC calls is a loud failure, not a silent one: the call is refused and the mapping data flow errors. Theobald documents that blocked calls surface an error message referencing SAP Note 3635619. Attaching the Note 3255746 block to a chapter whose whole premise is 'every pipeline stayed green' teaches the wrong triage reflex. Delete that clause. Source: https://helpcenter.theobald-software.com/xtract-is/knowledge-base/odp-restriction-opt-out/

THE SAP NOTE MAP IS INCOMPLETE AND SENDS A READER TO THE WRONG NOTE. The research names 3255746, 3439624 and 3731818 only. Theobald's page states SAP Note 3748819 introduces the security update that actually blocks unauthorized ODP-RFC access, 3731818 provides guidance and fixes to temporarily opt out, and 3635619 is the note referenced in the runtime error message. The opt-out is activated by running report RODPS_REPL_SECUREACCESS_OPTOUT through transaction SE38, which is the actionable artefact and is missing entirely from the research. SAPinsider separately reports Note 3439624 as a self assessment tool available since 13 April 2026, that is, a detection aid rather than an enforcement note. Matillion gives the enforcement date as 9 June 2026 and the opt-out expiry as December 2026. SCENARIO 3 PRESCRIBES A LANE THAT DOES NOT EXIST FOR HALF THE LIKELY ESTATE. It routes 'objects that already flow through BW' to the ADF SAP BW Open Hub connector. Microsoft states flatly on that connector page: 'SAP Business Warehouse version 7.01 or higher (in a recent SAP Support Package Stack released after the year 2015). SAP BW/4HANA isn't supported by this connector.' An estate on BW/4HANA, which is where SAP has been pushing customers for years, has no Open Hub lane in ADF at all. The triage has to branch on BW versus BW/4HANA. Source: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-sap-business-warehouse-open-hub

THE SAP TABLE CONNECTOR IS PRESENTED AS A COMPLIANCE HARBOUR WITHOUT EVIDENCE. The research calls it 'increasingly the non-ODP fallback' and scenario 3 asserts 'that path is plain RFC table reads and is not ODP'. The technical half is right, but Microsoft's own Important banner does not list the SAP Table connector among the alternatives 'not affected by SAP Note 3255746'; it lists four Fabric options only. Matillion quotes SAP's broader position: 'SAP's rules also state that technologies such as SLT Replication Server ... and SAP Database Trigger must not be used to move data out of SAP.' On top of that, the default function module is /SAPDS/RFC_READ_TABLE2, which sits in the SAP Data Services namespace. Present this lane as an open licensing question for the SAP contract owner, never as an engineering fact. NO FABRICATED PRODUCT SURVIVED THE HUNT, AND I AM SAYING SO RATHER THAN MANUFACTURING ONE. Every product name, transaction code, function module, program, note number and property in the research resolved against a vendor page: ODQMON, LTRC, SE38, RODPS_REPL_TEST, /SAPDS/RFC_READ_TABLE2, customRfcReadTableFunctionModule, SapHanaDynamicRange, ?AdfHanaDynamicRangePartitionCondition, PhysicalPartitionsOfTable, ODP contexts ABAP_CDS BW HANA SAPI SLT~ ODP_SELF RANDOM, run modes fullAndIncrementalLoad fullLoad incrementalLoad, SelfDependencyTumblingWindowTriggerReference, DMIS 2011 SP 05, NetWeaver 7.4 SPS 04. Even the odd lowercase 'PartitionOntime' is the literal spelling in Microsoft's own table, not a typo in the research. The closest thing to a misnaming is the Mirroring page title drift noted above.

products.name: SAP CDC connector (mapping data flow source)
products.vendor: Microsoft (Azure Data Factory / Azure Synapse Analytics)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Delta extraction from any ODP capable SAP system without watermark columns, and the only ADF SAP connector that surfaces deletes. The capabilities table lists Mapping data flow (source) only: no copy activity, no lookup. Requires an ADLS Gen2 staging linked service that 'cannot use a self-hosted integration runtime', and a Checkpoint Key unique per source. Microsoft reserves the staging folder: 'The staging folder should be considered an internal storage of the SAP CDC connector ... we recommend not to use the staging folder for other purposes.' Pointing Databricks Auto Loader at it is building on a format Microsoft can change. Current limitations are exactly two bullets: no resetting or deleting ODQ subscriptions from Data Factory, and no SAP hierarchies. In 2026 senior use is mostly exit planning: inventory subscriptions, prove the alternative, decommission cleanly in ODQMON.

products.name: Self-hosted integration runtime (SHIR)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The only way ADF reaches an on-premises or network isolated SAP system. Four senior concerns, each quoted from Learn: 'You can have up to four nodes associated with a self-hosted integration runtime'; the node 'encrypts the credentials by using Windows Data Protection Application Programming Interface (DPAPI) and saves the credentials locally', synchronised across nodes when several are set for high availability; 'Each version of self-hosted integration runtime expires in one year', warned 90 days ahead, and on expiry 'it will display an offline status and no longer work properly'; and a data flow staging store cannot route through it. Sizing anchor: 'a 2-GHz processor with 4 cores, 8 GB of RAM, and 80 GB of available hard drive space'. Throughput anchor, quoted exactly: 'an internal test achieved a higher than 12-MB/s throughput when running parallel extractions on a self-hosted integration runtime computer that has 16 CPU cores.'

products.name: SAP Table connector
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Copy activity and lookup read of transparent, pooled and clustered tables and views over RFC, using /SAPDS/RFC_READ_TABLE2 or a customRfcReadTableFunctionModule with a matching import, export and tables interface. No delta semantics, so the engineer owns the watermark and never sees deletes. Partitioning is explicit: partitionOption of None, PartitionOnInt, PartitionOnCalendarYear, PartitionOnCalendarMonth, PartitionOnCalendarDate or PartitionOntime (the lowercase t is Microsoft's own spelling), with maxPartitionsNumber defaulting to 1 and 'strongly recommended' to be a multiple of parallelCopies. Also the only ADF SAP connector that will join tables, through a custom function module fed a join statement as rfcTableOptions. Do not present it as a sanctioned escape from SAP Note 3255746: Microsoft does not list it among the unaffected alternatives, and SAP's stated position on third party extraction is broader than ODP alone.

products.name: SAP BW Open Hub connector
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Reads an Open Hub Destination local table after a DTP has written into it, using request IDs as the delta boundary via excludeLastRequest (default true) and baseRequestId. The value is that SAP owns the delta and ADF only advances a request pointer. Three hard rules, verbatim from Microsoft: the OHD must be type Database Table with the Technical Key option checked; 'it's not allowed to have request IDs from different DTPs in the same Open Hub table. Therefore, you must not create more than one DTP for each Open Hub Destination', so full and delta from one InfoProvider need two OHDs; and 'SAP BW/4HANA isn't supported by this connector', which removes this lane entirely for a BW/4HANA estate.

products.name: SAP HANA connector
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: SQL level read of HANA row and column tables and information models (analytic and calculation views) through the HANA ODBC driver on a SHIR, with Basic or Windows authentication. Heavy parallel loads use partitionOption PhysicalPartitionsOfTable (table only, not query) or SapHanaDynamicRange with the ?AdfHanaDynamicRangePartitionCondition placeholder hooked into the WHERE clause; packetSize defaults to 2048 KB. Note the page contradicts itself on sink support: the capabilities table says source/sink, the prose says 'the SAP HANA connector is not supported as sink' and routes writes through the generic ODBC connector, whose linked service is 'with different type thus cannot be reused'. Decide which half you trust before the booklet ships.

products.name: SAP Landscape Transformation Replication Server (SLT)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Trigger based CDC on SAP application tables and simple views, used as an ODP proxy so tables (not just extractors and CDS views) can feed the operational delta queue. Microsoft is explicit that it is optional: 'SLT is only required if you want to replicate data from SAP tables with the SAP CDC connector. All other sources work out-of-the-box without SLT.' Needs NetWeaver 7.4 SPS 04 or later plus the DMIS 2011 SP 05 add-on, configured in transaction LTRC with an RFC destination as source, RFC Connection as target, scenario Operational Data Provisioning (ODP), and a Queue Alias entered in the format SLT~<your queue alias> which becomes the ADF ODP context. Matillion reports SAP's rules as also prohibiting SLT Replication Server and SAP Database Trigger for moving data out of SAP, which is a question for your SAP licensing contact rather than your architect.

products.name: Operational Data Provisioning framework and transaction ODQMON
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The provider and subscriber machinery the whole CDC story rests on: providers produce full or incremental data into an operational delta queue, and the mapping data flow source is a subscriber. ODQMON is where the senior work happens. Filter by the Subscriber name from the linked service, set Request Selection to All, use wildcards in Queue to find a table (Microsoft's own example is EKKO), tick Calculate Data Volume to compare SAP side rows and bytes against ADF, open a subscription to see the request list that maps one to one onto data flow runs, and delete subscriptions no longer needed 'so SAP systems can stop tracking their subscription states and remove the unconsumed data packages from the ODQ'. Setup validation harness is program RODPS_REPL_TEST. The 2026 opt-out is a different report, RODPS_REPL_SECUREACCESS_OPTOUT, run through SE38.

products.name: SAP Connector for Microsoft .NET (SAP NCo 3.0), 64 bit
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The RFC client library every RFC based ADF SAP connector loads. Must be installed on each SHIR node with Install Assemblies to GAC selected in the Optional setup steps dialog; the SAP CDC, SAP Table and SAP BW Open Hub pages each repeat the requirement independently. It is the classic cause of a node that registers fine and then fails only on SAP activities, which is why SHIR nodes are not interchangeable commodity VMs: build them from an image, not by hand. Minimum SHIR versions differ by connector (3.17 or later for SAP Table, 3.13 or above for Open Hub), so a fleet on mixed versions can fail one connector and not another.

products.name: SAP Datasphere with Premium Outbound Integration
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: SAP's sanctioned egress path now that ODP RFC is closing. A Datasphere replication flow extracts the initial snapshot plus changed records and lands them in an ADLS Gen2 container, and Microsoft confirms it 'supports all types of SAP sources offered by SAP Datasphere, including SAP S/4HANA, SAP ECC, SAP BW/4HANA, SAP BW, and SAP Datasphere itself'. The commercial fact governs: 'SAP Datasphere Premium Outbound Integration pricing applies when mirroring SAP data via SAP Datasphere.' That converts an engineering choice into a volume based licensing negotiation, and it is the number to get from SAP before any architecture is committed. The rename from SAP Data Warehouse Cloud is single sourced and should be presented as such.

products.name: Tumbling window trigger
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The only ADF trigger with state, retry and dependency semantics, and the one Microsoft prescribes for SAP CDC: 'Set Max concurrency to 1' and add a self dependency 'so that a subsequent pipeline run always waits until earlier pipeline runs are successfully completed'. One to one with a single pipeline. Constraints quoted from the two trigger pages: maxConcurrency is 'An integer between 1 and 50'; 'The minimum window interval is 5 minutes'; frequency allows Minute, Hour or Month; 'After a tumbling window trigger is published, the interval and frequency values can't be edited'; 'A tumbling window trigger can depend on a maximum of five other triggers'; and 'A tumbling window trigger waits on dependencies for seven days before timing out. After seven days, the trigger run fails.' Self dependency offset is mandatory and must be negative.

products.name: Mapping data flows on Azure Integration Runtime (Spark)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Mandatory for SAP CDC because the ODP change feed carries technical attributes such as ODQ_CHANGEMODE and 'an extract of change data from ODP can contain multiple changes to the same key', so order must be respected while processing in parallel. Tuning levers, all quoted from Learn: cluster size from 4 worker plus 4 driver cores (small) through 256 worker plus 16 driver (272 total); shuffle partitions settable 'from 50 up to 2000' at 'approximately 1.5 GB of data per partition', default 200 which suits roughly 300 GB; and time to live to avoid a cold cluster start on sequential flows, with two traps, that 'Time to live isn't available when using the auto-resolve integration runtime (default)' and that only one job runs per cluster, which makes TTL counterproductive for parallel flows. Microsoft gives no numeric cold start figure, only 'a few minutes'.

products.name: The four named Fabric exits from ODP RFC: Mirroring for SAP Datasphere in Fabric, SAP Business Data Cloud Connect for Microsoft Fabric, Copy Job in Fabric for SAP with ABAP Add-on, and third party partner solutions with Open Mirroring in Fabric
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The exits Microsoft itself names on the SAP CDC architecture page as 'not affected by SAP Note 3255746'. Mirroring for SAP Datasphere is Generally Available and runs Datasphere replication flow to ADLS Gen2 to OneLake, where the mirrored database handles conversion to Parquet and exposes Delta tables through an autogenerated SQL analytics endpoint. BDC Connect was 'Announced at Microsoft Ignite 2025, available later this year', with Microsoft explicitly warning to 'review the SAP terms and conditions regarding limitations on using this data in downstream data solutions', a live constraint on a Snowflake plus Databricks estate. The Copy Job with a Microsoft supplied ABAP Add-on is stated as 'publicly available at Microsoft Build 2026' and deliberately does not use the ODP RFC API. The fourth option, SAP certified partner offerings with Open Mirroring, is the only one admitting a non Microsoft landing path and is the one the research dropped. The strategic point stands: all four land in Fabric.

senior_scenarios.title: Splitting a colliding delta subscription so the snapshot can be deferred past quarter close, not avoided
senior_scenarios.narrative:
A finance extractor over ABAP_CDS with roughly 1.4 billion rows has run fullAndIncrementalLoad on a 15 minute tumbling window for two years. Its Checkpoint Key was parameterised across a data flow that also serves three other sources and the values were never made unique, so the states have collided. You cannot repair a Checkpoint Key: changing it starts a fresh change data capture process. Be honest about what the fix costs. Any route back to a correct state re-extracts a full snapshot of this object. What you get to choose is when that snapshot runs and whether you lose deltas while it runs.

The move is to decouple the two halves of the run mode. First publish a data flow in incrementalLoad mode with a new unique Checkpoint Key and let it run once. Microsoft: incremental changes only 'creates an ODP delta subscription without returning an initial full data snapshot in the first run'. From that instant every change accumulates in the operational delta queue, so the clock is protected before you have moved a single row of history.

Only then schedule the fullLoad data flow, outside quarter close, partitioned in the Optimize tab with Partition type Source. Partition conditions are SAP selection options expressed in JSON, and Microsoft's own example splits on fiscal year: {"fieldName": "GJAHR", "sign": "I", "option": "BT", "low": "2011", "high": "2015"}. Full mode 'extracts a current full data snapshot without initiating a change data capture process', so it cannot disturb the subscription you just opened.

Merge on the declared Key columns, newest wins, snapshot as base, accumulated deltas replayed on top. Confirm in ODQMON by Subscriber name that exactly one live subscription remains and delete the old one so SAP stops retaining unconsumed packages.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The instinctive move, reset and let fullAndIncrementalLoad re-initialise, loses every change that occurs while the multi day snapshot runs, with no way to reconstruct them. The safe move requires knowing that incrementalLoad opens a subscription without a snapshot, that fullLoad establishes no CDC process and therefore cannot corrupt one, and that ODQ retains from subscription creation rather than snapshot completion. Nothing in the ADF interface signals that the ordering matters. Partition conditions are unchecked by ADF, which states outright that it is the user's responsibility to ensure conditions do not overlap, so a badly split GJAHR range silently double counts. Values must be in SAP internal format with leading zeroes and dates as eight character YYYYMMDD strings.

senior_scenarios.title: An ODP extractor whose deltas stopped after an SAP transport, while every pipeline stayed green
senior_scenarios.narrative:
A transport goes into production on a Tuesday night. From Wednesday the sales pipeline still runs every 15 minutes, every tumbling window succeeds, the data flow reports success, Power BI keeps refreshing, and row counts plateau. Nobody is paged, because ADF has nothing to fail on. An empty delta is a valid delta.

The diagnosis lives on the SAP side. In ODQMON, filter by the Subscriber name configured on the SAP CDC linked service, set Request Selection to All, open the queue by table name, and compare the subscription's request list against the data flow run history, since 'a list of requests corresponds to mapping data flow runs in Data Factory'. Tick Calculate Data Volume to get SAP side rows and bytes. If requests stop appearing, ADF is polling a queue nobody is filling: the transport re-imported a DataSource and dropped its release for ODP extraction (Microsoft cites SAP Note 2232584 for releasing extractors for the ODP API), or it changed a CDS view so extractions no longer populate the ODQ (SAP Note 3038236, listed by Microsoft under Known issues). If the requests are there with the expected counts, Microsoft's own instruction runs the other way and the loss is downstream, owned by ADF.

The trap during triage is the developer who reproduces it in debug mode and reports that it works. Debug runs use a different subscriber process value and therefore open a separate subscription inside SAP, and that value has a lifetime limited to the browser session. A green debug run proves nothing about the production subscription.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The failure sits on the far side of an organisational boundary and produces no error anywhere in Azure. Senior instinct has to be to reach for an SAP transaction rather than an ADF monitor, then to compare two independent row counts across systems rather than trusting either. The debug versus triggered subscriber process distinction is buried in an advanced topics page and is exactly the detail that turns a two hour incident into a two week one. Microsoft states the remedy plainly: to test stability over multiple days, publish and use triggered runs. Keep the 2026 ODP RFC block out of this chapter, because a blocked RFC call errors loudly rather than plateauing quietly, and conflating the two teaches the wrong reflex.

senior_scenarios.title: Getting off ODP RFC before the June 2026 block, with the warehouse split across Snowflake and Databricks
senior_scenarios.narrative:
Microsoft's SAP CDC architecture page now opens with an Important banner: a recent update of SAP Note 3255746 announces a security patch that blocks incoming calls to the ODP RFC API from third party clients including the ADF SAP CDC connector. Third party reporting puts technical enforcement at 9 June 2026, with a temporary opt-out activated by running report RODPS_REPL_SECUREACCESS_OPTOUT through SE38 per SAP Note 3731818, valid to the end of 2026. Confirm the notes and dates with your own SAP contacts; treat the direction as settled.

The senior work is triage, not tooling. Inventory every Checkpoint Key and every ODQMON subscription and map each to a business consumer, because a good share will be feeding a dashboard nobody opens. Then split what remains. Configuration and master data with no true delta need can move to the SAP Table connector with explicit partitioning and an owned watermark, provided the SAP contract owner signs off, because Microsoft does not name that connector as an unaffected alternative. Objects flowing through classic SAP BW 7.01 or higher can move to Open Hub, where the DTP owns the delta and ADF only advances a request ID, but confirm the release first: Microsoft states BW/4HANA is not supported by that connector, so a BW/4HANA estate has no Open Hub lane at all. Everything genuinely transactional and high volume goes to a sanctioned path: SAP Datasphere replication flows landing in ADLS Gen2, then into Snowflake or Databricks, priced under Premium Outbound Integration.

The uncomfortable part is that all four of Microsoft's named replacements land in Fabric, and this estate is Snowflake plus Databricks with Power BI on top.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The forcing function is a vendor security and licensing decision, so no amount of ADF skill avoids it. The migration must be sequenced against a hard date, on objects whose delta history cannot be reconstructed once a subscription is deleted, while an SAP basis team applies support packages on its own calendar. Two of the three fallback lanes carry conditions most teams discover late: Open Hub is unavailable on BW/4HANA, and the SAP Table lane is a licensing question rather than an engineering one. Premium Outbound Integration turns the remaining choice into a commercial negotiation, and the Fabric shaped alternatives conflict with a warehouse strategy already committed elsewhere. Deciding what to let die is the highest value work here and no tool does it for you.

silent_failures.failure: Two SAP CDC sources share one Checkpoint Key, so one source's change data capture state overwrites the other's. Both pipelines keep succeeding and both keep returning plausible looking deltas.
silent_failures.why_invisible: There is no uniqueness constraint and no warning. Microsoft only says it is 'important to use a unique Checkpoint Key for each source. Otherwise status information of one source will be overwritten by another source.' The symptom is missing rows for one object, not an error, and the two data flows may be owned by different people. A unique ID is generated by default, so this only bites when someone deliberately parameterises the key, which is precisely the metadata driven pattern Microsoft recommends for hundreds of sources. Related trap: the Checkpoint Key property is not shown at all when Run mode is Full on every run, so it can silently vanish and reappear as a fresh key when someone toggles run mode.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A reconciliation, not a monitor. For each object, compare Rows copied in the ADF data flow monitor against the request row counts under the matching subscription in ODQMON, filtered by the linked service Subscriber name, over the same window. Independently, assert uniqueness as a build gate: extract every checkpointKey value from the pipeline JSON in the collaboration branch and fail the pull request if the sorted list has duplicates. That is a grep that must return empty, and it runs in CI rather than in someone's head.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-sap-change-data-capture (Transform data with the SAP CDC connector) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics (Parameterizing the Checkpoint Key)

silent_failures.failure: A developer validates a CDC change in debug mode, sees correct data, and ships. The published triggered pipeline behaves differently because it uses a different ODP subscription.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Debug and triggered runs use different subscriber process values, so they 'create separate subscriptions (that is, change data capture processes) within the SAP system'. The debug subscriber process value also has 'a life time limited to the browser UI session'. A debug run therefore tests a subscription that will not exist tomorrow and that has none of production's accumulated state. The output looks identical to a correct production run, which is why it is trusted. The same mechanism makes incident triage misleading: reproducing in debug appears to prove the pipeline is healthy while the production subscription is dead.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A rehearsal, in the literal sense Microsoft prescribes: 'To test stability of a change data capture process with SAP CDC over a longer period of time (say, multiple days), data flow and pipeline need to be published, and triggered runs need to be executed.' Make a multi day triggered soak on a non production factory a merge requirement for any CDC change, and verify in ODQMON that the subscription under the production subscriber process advanced across that period. A single green debug run is not evidence and should not be accepted as one in review.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics (Debugging)

silent_failures.failure: An SAP BW Open Hub feed is permanently one DTP request behind, or skips and replays rows, because excludeLastRequest defaults to true and someone created a second DTP writing into the same Open Hub Destination.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The default is deliberate and correct: excluding the last request is what lets ADF read a table the DTP may still be writing into, and Microsoft says so, 'this procedure ensures that no rows get lost caused by the asynchronous extraction'. But it means the warehouse is structurally never fully current, which surfaces as a staleness complaint rather than a configuration fact. The multiple DTP case is worse: request IDs from different DTPs interleave in one Open Hub table and the baseRequestId pointer stops meaning what the pipeline assumes, with no error. Microsoft states the rule flatly: 'it's not allowed to have request IDs from different DTPs in the same Open Hub table. Therefore, you must not create more than one DTP for each Open Hub Destination.' Note also that the page names the property both excludeLastRequestId and excludeLastRequest; the JSON key is excludeLastRequest.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A second derivation plus a row count. Reconcile the target against the source InfoProvider for a closed period, not against the Open Hub table, since that table shares the defect. Separately, run a control query over the Open Hub table grouped by DTP request ID to prove exactly one DTP has ever written to it, and assert that the max request ID copied in the last run matches the stored watermark. Also check the DTP's SAP HANA Execution flag: Microsoft documents that leaving it on means 'only subset of data is copied over using copy activity (1 million rows)' because the service can only retrieve the first batch, with no failure raised.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-sap-business-warehouse-open-hub (Delta extraction flow; Troubleshooting tips)

silent_failures.failure: Rows calculated is lower than Rows copied in the data flow monitor, and someone fixes the phantom data loss. The genuinely dangerous inverse is wrongly declared Key columns.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The gap looks exactly like rows being dropped in transit and the two numbers sit side by side in the monitor, but it is correct behaviour: 'after extracting the changed data records from the SAP system, the data flow performs a deduplication of the changed rows based on the key definition. Only the most recent record is passed further down the data flow.' The real failure is silent and inverse. Microsoft's own key example is SAP table VBAP with ["VBELN", "POSNR"], or ["MANDT","VBELN","POSNR"] where the client field matters. Declare VBELN alone, or drop MANDT in a multi client system, and deduplication collapses distinct business rows into one while the counts still look reasonable.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A second derivation of the key. Prove uniqueness at source before trusting the sink: run count versus distinct count on the declared key columns over a full snapshot and require exact equality. Then reconcile a closed period end to end, source system total against warehouse total, rather than eyeballing Rows copied against Rows calculated. Treat any divergence between count and distinct count as a blocking defect in the Key columns definition, not as a data quality observation.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-management (Monitor SAP CDC data flows) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-advanced-topics (Key columns)

silent_failures.failure: A self-hosted integration runtime node passes its one year version expiry, or a high availability pair drifts out of credential sync, and SAP extraction degrades rather than stopping.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Microsoft states that 'Each version of self-hosted integration runtime expires in one year' and that on expiry the node 'will display an offline status and no longer work properly'. In a gateway of up to four nodes the survivors absorb the load, so throughput drops and timeouts appear intermittently while the logical integration runtime still looks healthy enough to run. The credential case is nastier: each node encrypts credentials with Windows DPAPI and stores them locally, with synchronisation across nodes handled transparently, so if sync has quietly failed everything works until a failover and then activities fail on credential access in a way that reads like an SAP authorisation problem. Auto update masks version drift by design, since Microsoft pushes 'an auto-update every three months, using a stable version from the preceding three months', not the latest.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A row count over your own estate, run on a schedule rather than after an incident. Microsoft publishes a script on the auto update page that logs in with az, enumerates every factory and every SelfHosted integration runtime, reads each one's version, and prints an expiring or expired list. Run it monthly and require that list to be empty; the 90 day expiry warning gives you the window. For high availability, assert credential sync across nodes before declaring one healthy, prefer Azure Key Vault backed linked services so credentials are not stored on the nodes at all, and verify failover by actually failing a node over in a maintenance window.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/self-hosted-integration-runtime-auto-update (Self-hosted Integration Runtime Expire Notification; Autoupdate version vs latest version) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/create-self-hosted-integration-runtime (High availability and scalability; Credential sync)

silent_failures.failure: The tumbling window trigger runs CDC windows concurrently, or a backfill fires hundreds of windows at once, and deltas are applied out of order.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The trigger and every pipeline run report success. maxConcurrency accepts any integer between 1 and 50 and is easy to leave at the sample value of 50, and if startTime is in the past then 'based on the formula M=(CurrentTime- TriggerStartTime)/TumblingWindowSize, the trigger generates {M} backfill(past) runs in parallel, honoring trigger concurrency, before executing the future runs'. Each window pulls whatever is currently in the operational delta queue, so two windows running at once against one subscription do not partition the change stream cleanly, they race it. The sink ends up looking internally consistent and being wrong. Microsoft's SAP CDC guidance is explicit and is the step people skip: set Max concurrency to 1 and add a self dependency.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A configuration assertion plus a reconciliation against an ordering invariant. Assert in CI that every trigger referencing an SAP CDC pipeline has maxConcurrency of 1 and a dependsOn entry of type SelfDependencyTumblingWindowTriggerReference with a negative offset, since Microsoft states self dependency 'should always be a negative offset'; that is a JSON check that must return empty on violation. Then prove ordering empirically: pick business keys that changed several times inside one window and confirm the sink holds the last state. Before enabling any trigger whose startTime is in the past, compute M by hand and follow Microsoft's own recommendation to do an initial historical load instead of letting the trigger backfill a long period.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/how-to-create-tumbling-window-trigger (Execution order of windows in a backfill scenario; maxConcurrency) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/sap-change-data-capture-management (Run an SAP data replication pipeline on a recurring schedule)

silent_failures.failure: A non Key Vault linked service or integration runtime JSON is published to the live service the moment it is created, so Git and the running factory disagree and the publish branch goes stale.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The interface accepts everything and the collaboration branch looks like the truth. Microsoft lists the exact scenarios: a user deletes a non AKV linked service in a feature branch that is never merged, since 'non-AKV linked services are published immediately regardless of whether they're in Git'; a user modifies the factory using the SDK or PowerShell; a user moves all resources to a new branch and publishes for the first time; a user uploads a non AKV linked service or integration runtime JSON manually and references it from a dataset, where 'the user interface allows it because it exists in the Git environment. It will be rejected at publish time since it doesn't exist in the data factory service.' Each produces a deployed state that differs from main with no failing build to show for it.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A reconciliation between Git and the live service, run as a scheduled job rather than at release time. Export the live factory definition through the REST API or PowerShell and diff it against the collaboration branch; any non empty diff outside expected Key Vault indirection is a finding. Two documented remedies point in opposite directions, so choose deliberately and record which is authoritative: Overwrite live mode treats the repository as source of truth (collaboration branch to live mode), while disconnecting and reconnecting Git treats live mode as source of truth (live mode to collaboration branch). Also use the repo setting that greys out the Publish button in ADF Studio once an automated release pipeline owns publishing, which Microsoft says 'helps you avoid overwriting the last automated publish deployment'.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control (Stale publish branch; Using passwords from Azure Key Vault; Editing repo settings)

corrections_to_my_facts: Mostly right, but the attribution is off on one point. The sentence 'the main branch is not representative of what is deployed' is not on the CI/CD page. It is on the Source control page, verbatim: 'The main branch isn't representative of what's deployed in the Data Factory service. The main branch *must* be published manually to the Data Factory service.' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control). Worth citing precisely because a reviewer will look for it on the wrong page.

'Publishing is manual' is true only of the classic flow, and Microsoft no longer presents it as the only flow. Under the automated publish flow the manual Publish button step is removed entirely: the build pipeline runs the npm package and produces the ARM template as a build artifact, and 'the DevOps release definition now consumes this new build pipeline instead of the Git artifact.' Microsoft states both are supported: 'You can continue to use the existing mechanism, which is the adf_publish branch, or you can use the new flow. Both are supported.' If you adopt automated publish you should also tick the repo setting that greys out the Publish button, which the docs describe as helping 'avoid overwriting the last automated publish deployment.' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-improvements, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control)

publish_config.json and publishBranch are correct, but two operational caveats are missing and both bite teams. First: 'Azure Data Factory can only have one publish branch at a time. When you specify a new publish branch, Data Factory doesn't delete the previous publish branch. If you want to remove the previous publish branch, delete it manually.' A stale abandoned publish branch left wired to an old release trigger is a live deployment source. Second: 'Data Factory only reads the publish_config.json file when it loads the factory. If you already have the factory loaded in the portal, refresh the browser to make your changes take effect.' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control)

'Non-Key-Vault linked services publish immediately regardless of branch' is correct and the docs are blunter than your phrasing. Source control says 'Any changes to Linked Services containing secrets such as passwords are published immediately to the Azure Data Factory service', and the stale-publish-branch troubleshooting section says '(non-AKV linked services are published immediately regardless of whether they're in Git)'. The reason given is that 'the credentials need to be encrypted'. (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control)

Add one item to your ADF Git list that is newer than most write-ups and matters for a Git-backed estate: the custom parameters page now carries a warning that 'The encryptedCredential property in linked service definitions is encrypted using the source factory's encryption key and is not transferable between factories. If your source-controlled linked service JSON files contain encryptedCredential, deployment to any other factory will fail or produce non-functional linked services.' It tells you to remove the property before committing and to use an AzureKeyVaultSecret reference or ManagedServiceIdentity instead. (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-resource-manager-custom-parameters)

Your list says the pre/post script stops triggers. There are two scripts and they behave differently, which changes the risk profile. PrePostDeploymentScript.ps1 stops and starts all triggers. Microsoft's note: 'Use the PrePostDeploymentScript.Ver2.ps1 if you would like to turn off/ on only the triggers that have been modified instead of turning all triggers off/ on during CI/CD.' Ver2 is the narrower blast radius and the larger silent-failure surface. Also two warnings people skip: 'Make sure to use PowerShell Core in ADO task to run the script' and 'If you don't use the latest versions of PowerShell and Data Factory module, you might run into deserialization errors.' (https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-sample-script)
