products.name: Azure Repos (Git) branch policies and cross-repo policies
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Server-side merge governance that a PR author cannot edit. The set is: require a minimum number of reviewers, check for linked work items, check for comment resolution, limit merge types, build validation, status checks, and automatically included reviewers. Path filters are supported on build validation, status checks and automatic reviewers, using absolute paths or wildcards, semicolon separated, with a leading ! for exclusion, evaluated left to right (example: /WebApp/*;!/WebApp/Tests/*). Cross-repo policies let you 'Protect the default branch of each repository' or 'Protect current and future branches matching a specified pattern' from Project settings, All Repositories, Policies. Bypass is two distinct permissions: 'Bypass policies when completing pull requests' and 'Bypass policies when pushing'.

products.name: GitHub repository rulesets
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The layered successor to branch protection. Up to 75 rulesets per repository, targeted by fnmatch pattern, and critically they compose rather than override: 'multiple rulesets can apply at the same time' and 'where multiple different versions of the same rule exist, the result is that the most restrictive version of the rule applies'. Anyone with read access can view active rulesets, which is a real audit win over admin-only branch protection. Push rulesets are the piece with no Azure Repos analogue at the same granularity: restrict file paths, file extensions, file path length and file size, applied to a private or internal repo and its entire fork network without branch targeting.

products.name: CODEOWNERS
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: In-repo, version-controlled, branch-scoped ownership of paths, placed in .github/, root or docs/ (first found wins), gitignore-style patterns where 'the last matching pattern takes the most precedence'. Paired with the ruleset option to require review from Code Owners. Two traps for a data estate: 'When reviews from code owners are required, an approval from any of the owners is sufficient', so a broad team entry dilutes ownership to nothing; and negation with ! does not work, so you cannot carve exceptions the way you would in .gitignore. GitHub advises owning the file itself (/.github/CODEOWNERS @owner) so ownership cannot be quietly edited in a PR.

products.name: Azure Pipelines environments, approvals and checks
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Promotion control that lives outside the YAML: 'Approvals and other checks aren't defined in the yaml file. Users modifying the pipeline yaml file can't modify the checks performed before start of a stage.' Checks attach to environments, service connections, repositories, variable groups, secure files and agent pools. Five categories run in order: static checks (Branch control, Required template, Evaluate artifact), pre-check approvals, dynamic checks (Approval, Invoke Azure Function, Invoke REST API, Business Hours, Query Azure Monitor alerts), post-check approvals, then Exclusive lock. For a data estate the load-bearing ones are Branch control (fully qualified refs/heads/<branch>, can require the branch be protected), Required template (a pipeline fails if it does not extend the referenced template), and Exclusive lock with lockBehavior sequential or runLatest to stop two releases hitting one factory at once.

products.name: GitHub Actions environments with deployment protection rules
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The Actions equivalent of an Azure Pipelines environment gate: up to 6 required reviewers where 'only one of the required reviewers needs to approve the job for it to proceed', prevent self-review, a wait timer, an 'Allow administrators to bypass configured protection rules' toggle, and deployment branch or tag rules. Environment secrets are 'only available to workflow jobs that use the environment' and are released 'only after any configured rules (for example, required reviewers) pass', which is the mechanism that keeps a prod service principal or prod parameter file out of reach of a lower-environment job. Plan constraint worth knowing before you design around it: GitHub Free can only configure environments for public repositories.

products.name: @microsoft/azure-data-factory-utilities (ADFUtilities npm package)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Turns 'Validate all' and 'Export ARM template' into CLI commands so the ARM template is produced by a build, not by a human clicking Publish. Two commands: npm run build validate <rootFolder> <factoryId> and npm run build export <rootFolder> <factoryId> [outputFolder], where factoryId is the full /subscriptions/.../factories/<name> resource id. Requires a package.json with the dependency at ^1.0.0 and, per the docs, 'Node.js version 20.x'. Export runs validation before generating. Two facts people miss: 'The ARM template generated isn't published to the live version of the factory', and 'The generated artifacts already contain pre- and post-deployment scripts for the triggers, so you don't need to add them manually.' Stop and start of only updated triggers 'is now generally available and is merged into the preceding command'.

products.name: ADF pre- and post-deployment PowerShell script (PrePostDeploymentScript.ps1 / .Ver2.ps1)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Stops triggers before the ARM deployment and restarts them after, and deletes resources removed from the factory. Argument shape is exact and asymmetric: predeployment is -predeployment $true -deleteDeployment $false, postdeployment is -predeployment $false -deleteDeployment $true, both alongside -armTemplate, -ResourceGroupName and -DataFactoryName. Run through AzurePowerShell@5 with pwsh: True. Ver1 stops every trigger; Ver2 stops only modified triggers. The -deleteDeployment flag has nothing to do with the factory: it 'is used to specify the deletion of the ADF deployment entry from the deployment history in ARM'.

products.name: Azure Resource Manager service connection with workload identity federation
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Replaces service principal secrets in Azure Pipelines. Microsoft's recommendation is explicit: 'We recommend using workload identity federation with either an app registration or managed identity. Workload identity federation eliminates the need for secrets and secret management', and the secret-based options 'are available for backwards compatibility and edge cases and not recommended'. There is an in-place Convert button, with two hard preconditions: 'Azure DevOps originally created the service connection' and 'Only one project uses the service connection.' Reversible for seven days only. A bulk conversion PowerShell script is published (requires PowerShell 7.3 and Azure CLI). Separately, and this catches quarterly release trains: 'Azure Pipelines is starting to automatically disable service connections that haven't been used for 100 days.'

products.name: GitHub Actions OIDC to Azure (azure/login, federated credentials)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The Actions-side equivalent: 'OpenID Connect (OIDC) allows your GitHub Actions workflows to access resources in Azure, without needing to store the Azure credentials as long-lived GitHub secrets.' The job needs permissions: id-token: write, azure/login takes client-id, tenant-id and subscription-id with no client secret, and the recommended federated credential audience is api://AzureADTokenExchange. The subject claim is where promotion policy actually lives: repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME, repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH, repo:ORG/REPO:ref:refs/tags/TAG, repo:ORG/REPO:pull_request. Environment-scoped subjects are what stop a feature branch minting a prod token. Note the 2026 change: for repositories created after July 15, 2026 the sub uses immutable identifiers, repo:OWNER@OWNER-ID/REPO@REPO-ID:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH, so federated credentials written to the old string will not match on newly created repos.

products.name: ARM Template Deployment task and arm-template-parameters-definition.json
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The actual deployment mechanism, plus the file that decides what is overridable per environment. Deployment mode must be Incremental: 'In Complete deployment mode, resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the new Resource Manager template will be deleted.' The custom parameter file must be named arm-template-parameters-definition.json in the root folder of the branch, and 'You must use that exact file name.' Action syntax is <action>:<name>:<stype> where = keeps the source value as the parameter default, - keeps no default (making it a mandatory deployment input), and | is the Key Vault secret case. Hard ceiling: 256 ARM parameters, and a custom file 'doesn't change the ARM template parameter limit of 256'. Also 'A definition can't be specific to a resource instance. Any definition applies to all resources of that type.'

products.name: Azure Pipelines classic release gates
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Automated health signals on pre- and post-deployment conditions of a release stage, distinct from a human approval. Built-in gates: Invoke Azure Function, Query Azure Monitor alerts, Invoke REST API, Query work items, Check Azure Policy compliance. The controls that matter for a data estate are 'Delay before evaluation' (let the deployed factory reach steady state before you judge it), 'Time between re-evaluation of gates', 'Timeout after which gates fail', and the ordering switch: for post-deployment conditions the default is to 'evaluate gates and prompt for manual approvals only when all gates are successful'. All gates must succeed in the same sampling interval, which is the property that makes them useful as a post-promotion smoke test.

products.name: GitHub merge queue
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The capability Azure Repos has no equivalent for. It 'automat[es] pull request merges into a busy branch and ensuring the branch is never broken by incompatible changes' by building temporary branches that group each PR with the latest base branch plus the PRs ahead of it, then running required checks against that combination. Workflows must handle the merge_group event. Merge limits are configurable between 1 and 100 PRs per group. Required via the 'Require merge queue' protection setting on the base branch. Azure Repos offers auto-complete, which merges when policies pass but does not pre-validate the combined result, so on a busy ADF collaboration branch with 8 to 12 authors Azure Repos will let two individually-green PRs land a broken main.

senior_scenarios.title: The triggers that were never stopped, and the factory that ran itself half-deployed
senior_scenarios.narrative: A Thursday 18:00 release promotes 41 changed artifacts into the UAT factory: a reworked SAP staging dataset, six pipelines, and one tumbling window trigger whose recurrence is unchanged but whose referenced pipeline was rewritten. The team migrated to PrePostDeploymentScript.Ver2.ps1 six months ago to shorten the deployment window, because Ver2 turns off only the triggers that have been modified. The trigger JSON did not change, so Ver2 leaves it running. The ARM deployment is Incremental and not atomic: it applies resources in dependency order over roughly four minutes. At minute two the tumbling window trigger fires. It starts the new pipeline definition, which references a dataset whose new folderPath parameter has not landed yet, so the pipeline writes a full extract into the previous partition path. At minute three the ARM deployment fails on a managed private endpoint whose properties differ between environments, exactly the case Microsoft flags as a deployment failure. The release goes red. The postdeployment script never runs, so nothing restarts triggers and nothing deletes removed resources. The factory is now a mixture of old and new, the triggers are in a state nobody chose, and downstream Snowflake tables have one partition written by a pipeline version that exists in no branch.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: Every individual decision was correct and documented. Ver2 is Microsoft's own recommendation for shortening deployment windows. Incremental mode is Microsoft's own instruction. The failure comes from the interaction of three documented behaviours: Ver2 scopes trigger stops to changed trigger definitions, ARM incremental deployment applies resources progressively rather than atomically, and a failed release skips its postdeployment step. No single doc page warns about the combination, and a senior engineer reading any one page in isolation would sign this design off.
named_tools: Azure Data Factory tumbling window trigger

senior_scenarios.title: The production connection string that walked backwards into UAT
senior_scenarios.narrative: Someone adds a Snowflake linked service in dev, authenticated with a connection string rather than Key Vault because the vault entry was pending. The default parameterization template covers connectionString as |:-connectionString:secureString, so it is parameterized and carries no default. Fine. Two sprints later a platform engineer adds a custom arm-template-parameters-definition.json to bring an existing Databricks interactive cluster id under control, copies the default template as the docs suggest, and while tidying changes the Snowflake linked service's account host entry from - to = because a deployment failed on a missing mandatory parameter and = made it go green. That single character means keep the current value as the default value for the parameter. The current value is dev's. Nobody notices, because dev deploying dev's own value to dev is invisible. Then a hotfix is cut. Following Microsoft's hotfix procedure, an engineer exports the ARM template from a hotfix branch created off the last production commit, and manually checks it into adf_publish. The export reads arm-template-parameters-definition.json from whichever branch you are currently working on, not the collaboration branch. The hotfix branch predates the vault migration. The exported template bakes production's host as a default, the release does not override that parameter, and UAT starts reading production.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The parameterization file is the only file in the estate where one character silently changes whether a value is inherited from the source factory or must be supplied per environment, and both settings deploy successfully. The hotfix branch reading its own copy of the definition file is documented but unintuitive, and it means a template exported for a rollback can carry parameterization semantics that no longer match the release pipeline's override list. A definition can't be specific to a resource instance, so you cannot fix it for one linked service without changing every linked service of that type.
named_tools: ARM Template Deployment task override template parameters

senior_scenarios.title: Migrating ADF governance from GitHub to Azure Repos and losing path ownership without a single error
senior_scenarios.narrative: The estate consolidates on Azure DevOps because Boards and Pipelines already live there. On GitHub, ownership was a CODEOWNERS file: the SAP CDC pipelines owned by the integration pair, the Snowflake linked services owned by the platform lead, the Power BI dataset refresh pipelines owned by BI. A ruleset required Code Owner review, and because CODEOWNERS is a file, a PR that changed ownership was itself reviewable and travelled with the branch. Azure Repos has no CODEOWNERS file. The nearest equivalent is the Automatically included reviewers branch policy with path filters, configured in Project settings, held server-side, invisible in the repo, unversioned, and identical across every branch. During the port an engineer writes the filter as ADFRoot/linkedService/* rather than /ADFRoot/linkedService/*. Azure Repos states plainly that a path in path filters that doesn't start with / or with a wildcard has no effect, and the path filter evaluates as if that path wasn't specified. The policy stays green in the settings UI. Every PR touching linked services now completes with no platform review, and nothing anywhere reports a problem.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The failure mode is a leading slash and a policy that reports as configured while matching nothing. Beyond the typo, the structural loss is real and not recoverable by configuration: ownership stops being a reviewable artifact in the repo and becomes project settings that only a policy administrator can see, so the ADF estate's ownership map is no longer under change control at the moment the team is largest. Cross-repo policies restore breadth but not versioning.
named_tools: GitHub rulesets (require review from Code Owners)
Azure Repos Automatically included reviewers policy

silent_failures.failure: A path filter on a branch policy (build validation, status checks, or automatically included reviewers) that does not begin with / or a wildcard matches nothing, so the policy is configured, displayed as On, and enforces nothing.
silent_failures.why_invisible: There is no validation error and no warning in the UI or the CLI. The policy list shows the policy as enabled and blocking. Pull requests complete cleanly, which is exactly what a correctly satisfied policy also looks like. The only observable difference between a working required-reviewer policy and a dead one is the absence of a reviewer nobody is looking for.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A deliberate canary pull request per protected path: touch one file under each governed folder and assert the expected reviewer or build appears in the PR Policies section. Automate it as a monthly rehearsal. Alternatively enumerate policies with az repos policy list and az repos policy show and assert every filenamePatterns entry starts with / or *, as a CI check on the settings export.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies (sections: Use path filters with branch policies; FAQ: What happens when a path filter doesn't start with / or a wildcard)

silent_failures.failure: Users holding Bypass policies when completing pull requests merge changes that fail required policies, and the pull request still displays the failure.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Microsoft states that for users who have bypass policy permissions, the reported policy status is advisory only. The PR shows a red policy, then completes anyway. A reviewer skimming a merged PR sees a failed check next to a successful merge and reads it as a flaky build rather than as an enforcement bypass, because both look identical in the timeline.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: Reconcile, monthly, the set of completed PRs against their final policy evaluation status, and separately audit who holds Bypass policies when completing pull requests and Bypass policies when pushing at project, repo and branch scope. On GitHub the equivalent is auditing ruleset bypass lists. A non-zero count of merged-with-failing-policy PRs is the number to drive to zero, and it must be counted, not estimated.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies (sections: Allow policy bypass when needed; FAQ: I have bypass policy permissions. Why do I still see policy failures?)

silent_failures.failure: A custom ARM parameterization entry set to = pins the source factory's value as the parameter default, so any environment whose release does not explicitly override that parameter silently inherits the dev (or prod) value.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The ARM deployment succeeds. The linked service or trigger is structurally valid in the target factory. Pipelines run, activities go green, rows land. The only symptom is that the data came from or went to the wrong system, and if the two systems share a schema the row counts and column names look entirely normal. By contrast, - produces a mandatory input and fails loudly, which is why teams under deployment pressure drift towards =.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A post-deployment reconciliation that reads back the deployed linked service and dataset properties from the target factory (Get-AzDataFactoryV2LinkedService) and asserts each host, server, database, url and folderPath against an expected per-environment manifest, run as an Azure Pipelines gate before the stage is marked successful. Second derivation: diff the generated ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json against the release override list and fail if any parameter carries a non-empty defaultValue that no override replaces.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-resource-manager-custom-parameters (Custom parameter syntax: = means keep the current value as the default value for the parameter) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-automate-azure-pipelines (Override template parameters)

silent_failures.failure: A stale publish branch: adf_publish holds an ARM template older than the collaboration branch, so a green release deploys code that no longer matches main.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The release pipeline is triggered by check-ins to the publish branch, so a publish branch that has quietly stopped receiving updates simply stops triggering, or triggers on old content. Microsoft documents four causes, including deleting a non-Key-Vault linked service in an unmerged feature branch, modifying the factory via SDK or PowerShell, and manually uploading a non-AKV linked service JSON. In every case the ARM deployment reports success. The gap only surfaces when someone compares deployed behaviour to main by hand.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A scheduled freshness check that compares the commit the publish branch was generated from against the head of the collaboration branch, and fails if the publish branch is behind. Under the automated publish flow this failure mode goes away by construction, because the ARM template is generated from the collaboration branch on every build rather than by a human clicking Publish. Second derivation: a row-level reconciliation of resource counts between the exported template and the live factory via Get-AzDataFactoryV2Pipeline.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control (Troubleshooting Git integration: Stale publish branch) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-improvements (The new CI/CD flow)

silent_failures.failure: A GitHub Actions federated credential whose subject claim is written against the old sub format silently stops matching on repositories created after July 15, 2026, and, more dangerously, a subject scoped to a branch rather than an environment grants prod-capable tokens to any workflow run on that branch.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The branch-scoped case is the silent one. Authentication succeeds, azure/login reports success, the deploy runs. Nothing in the run log distinguishes a token minted from a reviewed environment deployment from one minted by a workflow_dispatch on the same branch by anyone with write access, because the subject claim is the only thing that differed and it is never printed. The immutable-sub case at least fails loudly at login.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: Enumerate every federated identity credential on the app registrations used for deployment and assert that each subject uses the repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME form, not :ref:refs/heads/. Then rehearse: run the deploy workflow from a feature branch without the environment and confirm it cannot obtain a token. Mirror the check on the Azure DevOps side by confirming service connections use WorkloadIdentityFederation rather than ServicePrincipal, using the same REST query as Microsoft's bulk conversion script.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc (subject claim formats and immutable sub for repositories created after July 15, 2026), https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/security-harden-deployments/oidc-in-azure, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/connect-to-azure

silent_failures.failure: PrePostDeploymentScript.Ver2.ps1 stops only modified triggers, so a trigger whose own JSON is unchanged keeps firing throughout an ARM deployment that rewrites the pipelines it invokes.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The deployment is green and shorter, which reads as an improvement. The trigger run that fired mid-deployment appears in ADF monitoring as an ordinary successful run, because it usually is successful: it just executed a pipeline definition that was mid-swap. The corrupted output is a normal-looking load into a normal-looking target, indistinguishable from a scheduled run five minutes earlier.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: Assert the invariant directly rather than trusting the script's scope: after the predeployment step, query trigger runtime state (Get-AzDataFactoryV2Trigger) and fail the stage if any trigger is Started before the ARM deployment begins. Then reconcile trigger run start times against the deployment's start and end timestamps for every release, and treat any overlap as an incident regardless of run status. An Exclusive lock check on the environment prevents the related case of two releases overlapping on one factory.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-sample-script and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-automate-azure-pipelines (Updating active triggers: Deployment can fail if you try to update active triggers)

silent_failures.failure: An Azure Resource Manager service connection is auto-disabled after 100 days of non-use, breaking a low-frequency promotion path (annual DR rehearsal, quarterly prod-only release, the rollback pipeline) at exactly the moment it is needed.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Not silent at run time, it fails loudly. It is silent in planning: nothing surfaces the countdown, and the connections most at risk are precisely the ones nobody exercises, so the failure is discovered inside an incident window rather than during normal work. Microsoft's own wording is that Azure Pipelines is starting to automatically disable service connections that haven't been used for 100 days.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A rehearsal rather than a check: run the rollback and DR promotion pipelines on a schedule inside the 100-day window against a scratch resource group, so the credential path is exercised by the calendar rather than by an outage. Supplement with a periodic REST enumeration of service connections and their last-used date, and alert past 70 days.

checked.area: Azure DevOps Repos and CI/CD for a data estate: adversarial re-verification of the Azure Repos vs GitHub governance, ADF publish/parameterization, approvals and gates, and OIDC/workload identity federation claims against vendor documentation (August 2026)
corrections_to_my_facts: YOUR OWN ADF GIT LIST SURVIVES INTACT. I re-opened https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control (page date 2026-07-29) and every element checks out verbatim: collaboration branch default main, publish branch default adf_publish, publish_config.json with publishBranch, 'The main branch isn't representative of what's deployed in the Data Factory service. The main branch *must* be published manually', 'Changes made via PowerShell or an SDK are published directly to the Data Factory service and aren't entered into Git', 'Any changes to Linked Services containing secrets such as passwords are published immediately', and the Stale publish branch troubleshooting section with its four causes including '(non-AKV linked services are published immediately regardless of whether they're in Git)'. No correction needed. I did NOT open SAP Help Portal or the ADF SAP CDC connector page, so your SAP CDC and SAP Integration Suite facts remain unverified by me, not confirmed.

MISATTRIBUTED QUOTE (research error). The research attributes 'If you don't use the latest versions of PowerShell and Data Factory module, you might run into deserialization errors' to https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-sample-script. It is not on that page. That page carries only one warning: 'Make sure to use **PowerShell Core** in ADO task to run the script'. The deserialization warning lives on https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-automate-azure-pipelines (section 'Updating active triggers') and is repeated on https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery (Best practices). A reviewer checking the cited page will not find it.

SCENARIO 1 IS INVERTED AND CANNOT HAPPEN AS NARRATED. The narrative has a trigger start 'the new pipeline definition, which references a dataset whose new folderPath parameter has not landed yet'. ADF's generated ARM template declares dependsOn from a pipeline to the datasets and linked services it references, so Resource Manager deploys linked services, then datasets, then pipelines. A pipeline cannot land before the dataset it references. The realistic and equally damaging version is the mirror image: the updated dataset lands first and the still-unreplaced pipeline (or a mid-flight run started by the trigger) executes against a dataset definition it was never tested with. The rest of the scenario is sound, and the managed private endpoint failure is real: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery states 'If a private endpoint already exists in a factory and you try to deploy an ARM template that contains a private endpoint with the same name but with modified properties, the deployment will fail.'

SCENARIO 2 NAMES A PROPERTY THAT DOES NOT EXIST ON A SNOWFLAKE LINKED SERVICE. There is no 'account host entry'. Per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/connector-snowflake, the current linked service type is SnowflakeV2 and the connection property is accountIdentifier ('The name of the account along with its organization. For example, myorg-account123'); the legacy type Snowflake used a JDBC connectionString. The docs' own V1-to-V2 migration section states 'The accountIdentifier, warehouse, database, schema and role properties are used to establish a connection instead of connectionstring property.' The word host does appear in ADF's default parameterization template, but it belongs to other connector families (SFTP, SAP, HDInsight-style linked services), not Snowflake.

SCENARIO 2 GETS THE PARAMETERIZATION EDIT BACKWARDS. Per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-resource-manager-custom-parameters, the default parameterization template already sets "host": "=" under Microsoft.DataFactory/factories/linkedServices "*". Nobody flips host 'from - to =' because it was never '-'. The only '-' entry in the docs' worked example is "existingClusterId": "-" in the Databricks interactive-cluster sample, which is exactly the file the scenario says the engineer was editing. Also, connectionString in the default template is "|:-connectionString:secureString": the action character is '|' (the Key Vault special case), not '-'; the leading '-' sits in the NAME field and only shortens the parameter name. The no-default behaviour is stated separately in prose, not implied by the '-'.

SCENARIO 2's ENDING IS IMPOSSIBLE. 'The exported template bakes production's host as a default... and UAT starts reading production.' Export ARM Template runs from ADF Studio, and per https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery only the development factory is attached to Git ('The test and production factories shouldn't have a git repository associated with them'). The hotfix procedure at https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-hotfix-environment has you create the hotfix branch from a commit of the COLLABORATION branch and switch the (development) factory to it, so '=' can only pin the development factory's value. The narrative even contradicts itself: it establishes that the pinned value is dev's, then ends with production's. The true failure is dev's value silently landing in UAT and prod, which is bad enough and is what the booklet should say.

SCENARIO 2 CONTRADICTS THE RULE IT CITES. It describes an edit to 'the Snowflake linked service's account host entry', i.e. one instance, while its own why_hard correctly quotes 'A definition can't be specific to a resource instance. Any definition applies to all resources of that type.' Parameterization is keyed by entity type and connector type ('*', 'AzureDataLakeStore', 'Odbc'), never by a named linked service.

A REAL SNOWFLAKE HAZARD THE RESEARCH MISSED, AND SHOULD REPLACE THE INVENTED ONE WITH. accountIdentifier does not appear anywhere in ADF's default parameterization template. So a SnowflakeV2 linked service's account identifier is hard-coded into the exported ARM template from the source factory and is NOT overridable per environment unless the team adds it to arm-template-parameters-definition.json. That is the same silent-wrong-system outcome, and it is the documented default rather than an invented typo.

THE MERGE QUEUE COMPARISON IS OVERSTATED. 'Azure Repos will let two individually-green PRs land a broken main' is not true where build validation is configured properly. https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies documents a build expiration setting, 'Immediately when <branch name> is updated: This option sets PR build policy status to failed whenever the branch is updated, and requeues a build. This setting ensures that the PR changes build successfully even if the protected branch changes.' The honest framing: Azure Repos invalidates and revalidates serially after the base moves; GitHub merge queue pre-validates the combined result of the PR plus everything ahead of it. That is a throughput and ordering difference, not an absence of protection.

EVERYTHING ELSE I TESTED HELD. Verified verbatim and unchanged: the path-filter FAQ ('A path in path filters that doesn't start with / or with a wildcard has no effect. The path filter evaluates as if that path wasn't specified.'), the bypass FAQ ('For users who have bypass policy permissions, the reported policy status is advisory only.') and both bypass permission names; the five check categories and every check named in them, plus 'Approvals and other checks aren't defined in the yaml file' and the six resource types checks attach to; lockBehavior runLatest (default) and sequential; all five built-in classic gates including Check Azure Policy compliance and Query work items, and the post-deployment ordering default; the 100-day service connection auto-disable, the two Convert preconditions, seven-day revert, and PowerShell 7.3 plus Azure CLI for the bulk script; Node.js 20.x, ^1.0.0, both npm commands, 'Both are supported', 'The ARM template generated isn't published to the live version of the factory', 'The generated artifacts already contain pre- and post-deployment scripts', and 'The ability to stop/start only the updated triggers is now generally available and is merged into the preceding command'; the 256 ARM parameter ceiling, the exact file name rule, the export-reads-your-current-branch behaviour, and the encryptedCredential warning; 75 rulesets per repository, 'the most restrictive version of the rule applies', read-access visibility, push rulesets over a private or internal repo and its fork network; CODEOWNERS in .github, root or docs with first-found-wins, last-matching-pattern precedence, any-one-owner approval, and no ! negation; merge queue 1 to 100 and the merge_group event; six environment reviewers, one approval sufficient, admin bypass toggle, environment secrets gated on rules, and GitHub Free limited to public repositories; and the OIDC immutable subject for repositories created after July 15, 2026 in the form repo:OWNER@OWNER-ID/REPO@REPO-ID:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH. Azure Repos still has no native CODEOWNERS as of August 2026.

products.name: Azure Repos (Git) branch policies, path filters and cross-repo policies
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Server-side merge governance a PR author cannot edit: require a minimum number of reviewers, check for linked work items, check for comment resolution, limit merge types, build validation, status checks, automatically included reviewers. Path filters are supported on build validation, status checks and automatic reviewers; absolute paths must start with / or a wildcard, are semicolon separated, use a leading ! for exclusion, and are applied left to right (/WebApp/*;!/WebApp/Tests/* includes all of /WebApp except /WebApp/Tests; !/WebApp/Tests/* alone specifies no files, since nothing is included first). Build validation carries a build expiration option, 'Immediately when <branch name> is updated', which fails and requeues the PR build whenever the protected branch moves. Cross-repo policies are configured from Project settings > Repositories > All Repositories > Policies, including protection of current and future branches matching a specified pattern (case sensitive, and the branch need not exist yet). Bypass is two distinct permissions: 'Bypass policies when completing pull requests' and 'Bypass policies when pushing'.

products.name: GitHub repository rulesets
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The layered successor to branch protection. Up to 75 rulesets per repository and 75 organization-wide rulesets. They compose rather than override: 'Multiple rulesets can apply at the same time' and where versions of the same rule conflict, 'the most restrictive version of the rule applies'. 'Anyone with read access to a repository can view the active rulesets for the repository', which is a genuine audit win over admin-only branch protection. Push rulesets are the piece with no Azure Repos analogue at the same granularity: restrict file paths, file path length, file extensions and file size across a private or internal repository and that repository's entire fork network, with no branch targeting.

products.name: CODEOWNERS
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: In-repo, version-controlled, branch-scoped ownership of paths. GitHub searches .github/, root and docs/ in that order and uses the first file it finds. Gitignore-style patterns where 'Order is important; the last matching pattern takes the most precedence'. Paired with the ruleset option to require review from Code Owners. Two traps for a data estate: when code owner review is required, 'an approval from any of the owners is sufficient to meet this requirement', so a broad team entry dilutes ownership to nothing; and three gitignore features do not work, escaping a leading # with a backslash, using ! to negate a pattern, and using [ ] to define a character range, so you cannot carve exceptions the way you would in .gitignore. Own the file itself so ownership cannot be quietly edited in a PR. Azure Repos still has no native CODEOWNERS equivalent as of August 2026.

products.name: Azure Pipelines environments, approvals and checks
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Promotion control that lives outside the YAML: 'Approvals and other checks aren't defined in the yaml file. Users modifying the pipeline yaml file can't modify the checks performed before start of a stage.' Checks attach to environments, service connections, repositories, variable groups, secure files and agent pools. Five categories, run in the order they were created within each category: static checks (Branch control, Required template, Evaluate artifact), pre-check approvals, dynamic checks (Approval, Invoke Azure Function, Invoke REST API, Business Hours, Query Azure Monitor alerts), post-check approvals, then Exclusive lock. For a data estate the load-bearing ones are Branch control (branch names must be fully qualified as refs/heads/<branch name>; a branch counts as protected if at least one policy applies), Required template (a pipeline fails if it does not extend the referenced template), and Exclusive lock with lockBehavior sequential or runLatest (runLatest is the default) to stop two releases hitting one factory at once. Evaluate artifact currently works with container image artifacts only.

products.name: GitHub Actions environments with deployment protection rules
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The Actions equivalent of an Azure Pipelines environment gate: up to 6 people or teams as required reviewers where 'Only one of the required reviewers needs to approve the job for it to proceed', prevent self-review, a wait timer in minutes, an 'Allow administrators to bypass configured protection rules' toggle, and deployment branch or tag rules. Environment secrets are 'only available to workflow jobs that use the environment' and are released only after configured rules pass, which is the mechanism keeping a prod service principal or prod parameter file out of reach of a lower-environment job. Plan constraint to design around: GitHub Free can only configure environments for public repositories; private repositories need GitHub Pro, Team or Enterprise.

products.name: @microsoft/azure-data-factory-utilities (ADFUtilities npm package)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Turns 'Validate all' and 'Export ARM template' into CLI commands so the ARM template is produced by a build, not by a human clicking Publish. Two commands: npm run build validate <rootFolder> <factoryId> and npm run build export <rootFolder> <factoryId> [outputFolder], where factoryId is the full /subscriptions/<subId>/resourceGroups/<rg>/providers/Microsoft.DataFactory/factories/<name> resource id. Requires a package.json with the dependency at ^1.0.0 and Node.js version 20.x ('Be sure to use Node.js version 20.x and its compatible version to avoid errors that can occur due to package incompatibility with older versions'). Export runs validation before generating. Two facts people miss: 'The ARM template generated isn't published to the live version of the factory' and 'The generated artifacts already contain pre- and post-deployment scripts for the triggers, so you don't need to add them manually.' Stop and start of only updated triggers 'is now generally available and is merged into the preceding command'.

products.name: ADF pre- and post-deployment PowerShell script (PrePostDeploymentScript.ps1 / PrePostDeploymentScript.Ver2.ps1)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Stops triggers before the ARM deployment, restarts them after, and deletes resources removed from the factory. Argument shape is exact and asymmetric: predeployment is -predeployment $true -deleteDeployment $false, postdeployment is -predeployment $false -deleteDeployment $true, both alongside -armTemplate, -ResourceGroupName and -DataFactoryName. Run through AzurePowerShell@5 with pwsh: True and azurePowerShellVersion: 'LatestVersion'. Ver1 stops every trigger; use Ver2 'if you would like to turn off/ on only the triggers that have been modified'. The -deleteDeployment flag has nothing to do with the factory: it 'is used to specify the deletion of the ADF deployment entry from the deployment history in ARM'. Microsoft warns separately that you must use PowerShell Core in the ADO task, and that stale PowerShell or Data Factory modules cause deserialization errors.

products.name: Azure Resource Manager service connection with workload identity federation
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Replaces service principal secrets in Azure Pipelines. Microsoft is explicit: 'We recommend using workload identity federation with either an app registration or managed identity. Workload identity federation eliminates the need for secrets and secret management', and the secret-based options 'are available for backwards compatibility and edge cases and not recommended'. There is an in-place Convert button with two hard preconditions: 'Azure DevOps originally created the service connection' and 'Only one project uses the service connection.' Reversible for seven days only. A bulk conversion PowerShell script is published (requires PowerShell 7.3 or newer plus Azure CLI; it flips authorization.scheme to WorkloadIdentityFederation via the serviceendpoint REST API). Separately, and this catches quarterly release trains: 'Azure Pipelines is starting to automatically disable service connections that haven't been used for 100 days.'

products.name: GitHub Actions OIDC to Azure (azure/login with federated credentials)
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The Actions-side equivalent of workload identity federation: no long-lived Azure credentials in GitHub secrets. The job needs permissions: id-token: write; azure/login takes client-id, tenant-id and subscription-id with no client secret; the recommended federated credential audience is api://AzureADTokenExchange. The subject claim is where promotion policy actually lives: repo:ORG-NAME/REPO-NAME:environment:ENVIRONMENT-NAME, repo:ORG-NAME/REPO-NAME:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH-NAME, repo:ORG-NAME/REPO-NAME:ref:refs/tags/TAG-NAME, repo:ORG-NAME/REPO-NAME:pull_request. Environment-scoped subjects are what stop a feature branch minting a prod token. Verified 2026 change: repositories created after July 15, 2026 use immutable identifiers in the subject, repo:OWNER@OWNER-ID/REPO@REPO-ID:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH (example repo:octo-org@123456/octo-repo@456789:ref:refs/heads/main), so federated credentials written against the old string will not match on newly created repos. Not applicable to GitHub Enterprise Server; older repos may opt in.

products.name: ARM Template Deployment task and arm-template-parameters-definition.json
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: The deployment mechanism plus the file that decides what is overridable per environment. Deployment mode must be Incremental: 'In Complete deployment mode, resources that exist in the resource group but aren't specified in the new Resource Manager template will be deleted.' The custom parameter file is created in the root folder of your git branch and 'You must use that exact file name.' Action syntax is <action>:<name>:<stype>, where = keeps the current value as the parameter default, - keeps no default (making it a mandatory deployment input), and | is the special case for secrets from Azure Key Vault for connection strings or keys. Hard ceiling: 256 ARM parameters, and a custom file 'doesn't change the ARM template parameter limit of 256'. And 'A definition can't be specific to a resource instance. Any definition applies to all resources of that type.' Two behaviours that bite: when publishing, ADF reads the file from the collaboration branch, but when exporting 'Data Factory reads this file from whichever branch you're currently working on, not the collaboration branch'; and the encryptedCredential property in linked service definitions is encrypted with the source factory's key, is not transferable, and must be removed before committing in favour of AzureKeyVaultSecret or ManagedServiceIdentity.

products.name: Azure Pipelines classic release gates
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Automated health signals on pre- and post-deployment conditions of a release stage, distinct from a human approval. Built-in gates: Invoke Azure Function, Query Azure Monitor alerts, Invoke REST API, Query work items, Check Azure Policy compliance. The controls that matter for a data estate are 'Delay before evaluation' (for post-deployment gates, the maximum of the time for the deployed app to reach a steady operational state, for tests to run, and for incidents to be logged), 'Time between re-evaluation of gates', and 'Timeout after which gates fail'. For post-deployment conditions the default ordering is to evaluate gates and prompt for manual approvals only when all gates are successful. The property that makes gates useful as a post-promotion smoke test: 'all the gates are periodically reevaluated until all of them are successful at the same time. The release execution and deployment doesn't proceed if all gates don't succeed in the same interval and before the configured timeout.'

products.name: GitHub merge queue
products.what_a_senior_person_uses_it_for: Pre-merge validation of the combined result, which Azure Repos does not have. A merge queue 'creates temporary branches with a special prefix to validate pull request changes', grouping each PR with the latest base branch and the PRs ahead of it, then running required checks against that combination. Workflows must use the merge_group event to trigger. Group size is configurable: 'Select the minimum and maximum number of pull requests to merge into the base branch at the same time (between 1 and 100).' Required via the 'Require merge queue' branch protection setting on the base branch. Azure Repos' nearest equivalents are auto-complete plus a build validation policy set to expire 'Immediately when <branch name> is updated', which invalidates and requeues PR builds after the base moves; that is serial revalidation rather than pre-validation of the combined result, so on a busy ADF collaboration branch with 8 to 12 authors it costs throughput rather than correctness.

senior_scenarios.title: The triggers that were never stopped, and the factory that ran itself half-deployed
senior_scenarios.narrative: A Thursday 18:00 release promotes 41 changed artifacts into the UAT factory: a reworked SAP staging dataset, six pipelines, and one tumbling window trigger whose recurrence is unchanged but whose referenced pipeline was rewritten. The team moved to PrePostDeploymentScript.Ver2.ps1 six months ago to shorten the deployment window, because Ver2 turns off only the triggers that have been modified. The trigger JSON did not change, so Ver2 leaves it running. The ARM deployment is Incremental and not atomic: it applies resources in dependency order, linked services then datasets then pipelines, over roughly four minutes. At minute two the reworked SAP staging dataset has landed but the pipeline that consumes it has not, because ADF's generated template makes the pipeline dependsOn the dataset. The tumbling window trigger fires and starts the still-old pipeline definition against the new dataset, whose folderPath and schema were changed for the new pipeline. It runs green and writes a full extract into a partition path nobody expects. At minute three the deployment fails on a managed private endpoint whose properties differ between environments, which Microsoft flags directly: a private endpoint with the same name but modified properties fails to deploy. The release goes red. The postdeployment script never runs, so the triggers Ver2 did stop stay stopped, and resources removed from the factory are never deleted. The factory is a mixture of old and new, and downstream Snowflake tables have one partition written by a pipeline-plus-dataset combination that exists in no branch.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: Every individual decision was correct and documented. Ver2 is Microsoft's own recommendation for shortening deployment windows. Incremental is Microsoft's own instruction. Dependency ordering is what makes ARM deployments safe, and here it is exactly what creates the window: the dataset must land before the pipeline, so there is a guaranteed interval in which a new dataset is paired with an old pipeline. Four documented behaviours interact (Ver2 scopes trigger stops to changed trigger definitions, ARM incremental deployment applies resources progressively, dependency ordering guarantees a mismatched interval, and a failed release skips its postdeployment step) and no single doc page warns about the combination. Note this is the research's scenario with its causality corrected: the original had the new pipeline running against a not-yet-deployed dataset, which ADF's dependsOn graph makes impossible.
named_tools: ARM Template Deployment task (Incremental deployment mode)
Azure Data Factory tumbling window trigger

senior_scenarios.title: One character in the parameterization file, and UAT quietly reads development
senior_scenarios.narrative: This is the research's scenario 2 repaired; the original named a Snowflake 'account host' property that does not exist and ended with UAT reading production, which the export path cannot produce. A platform engineer adds a custom arm-template-parameters-definition.json to bring an existing Azure Databricks interactive cluster id under control, copying Microsoft's own worked example, which adds "existingClusterId": "-" under Microsoft.DataFactory/factories/linkedServices "*". A UAT release then fails on a missing mandatory deployment input, because '-' means don't keep the default value, so the parameter has no default and must be supplied. Under time pressure the engineer changes '-' to '=', the release goes green, and nobody notices, because a development deployment inheriting development's own cluster id is invisible. The same file also governs a SnowflakeV2 linked service, and here the gap is structural rather than a typo: accountIdentifier appears nowhere in ADF's default parameterization template, so the development account identifier is baked into the exported template and is not overridable per environment at all. Weeks later a hotfix is cut. Following Microsoft's procedure, an engineer creates a hotfix branch from the last commit deployed to production, switches ADF Studio to it, fixes the bug, selects Export ARM Template and manually checks the result into adf_publish. The export reads arm-template-parameters-definition.json from whichever branch you are currently working on, not the collaboration branch, and the hotfix branch predates the fix to that file. The template ships development's cluster id and development's Snowflake account as defaults, the release overrides neither, and UAT and production start running against development compute and a development warehouse.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The parameterization file is the one place in the estate where a single character decides whether a value is inherited from the source factory or must be supplied per environment, and both settings deploy successfully. '-' fails loudly, which is precisely why teams under deployment pressure drift towards '='. The hotfix branch reading its own copy of the definition file is documented but unintuitive, so a template exported for a rollback can carry parameterization semantics that no longer match the release pipeline's override list. And because a definition cannot be specific to a resource instance, you cannot fix one linked service without changing every linked service matched by that type or the '*' wildcard. Add the encryptedCredential warning on the same page and the failure surface widens: a committed linked service carrying encryptedCredential will not deploy to another factory at all.
named_tools: Override template parameters (ARM Template Deployment task)

senior_scenarios.title: Migrating ADF governance from GitHub to Azure Repos and losing path ownership without a single error
senior_scenarios.narrative: The estate consolidates on Azure DevOps because Boards and Pipelines already live there. On GitHub, ownership was a CODEOWNERS file: the SAP CDC pipelines owned by the integration pair, the Snowflake linked services owned by the platform lead, the Power BI dataset refresh pipelines owned by BI. A ruleset required review from Code Owners, and because CODEOWNERS is a file, a PR that changed ownership was itself reviewable and travelled with the branch. Azure Repos has no CODEOWNERS file, still true in August 2026. The nearest equivalent is the Automatically included reviewers branch policy with path filters, configured in Project settings, held server-side, invisible in the repo, unversioned, and identical across every branch. During the port an engineer writes the filter as ADFRoot/linkedService/* rather than /ADFRoot/linkedService/*. Azure Repos states plainly in its FAQ that a path in path filters that doesn't start with / or with a wildcard has no effect, and the path filter evaluates as if that path wasn't specified, because such a path can't match the / the absolute file path starts with. The policy stays green in the settings UI. Every PR touching linked services now completes with no platform review, and nothing anywhere reports a problem. A second engineer, tidying up, writes an exclusion-only filter !/ADFRoot/tests/* on the build validation policy, which specifies no files at all, since nothing is included first.
senior_scenarios.why_hard: The failure mode is a leading slash and a policy that reports as configured while matching nothing, with no validation error in the UI or the CLI. Beyond the typo, the structural loss is real and not recoverable by configuration: ownership stops being a reviewable artifact in the repo and becomes project settings that only a policy administrator can see, so the ADF estate's ownership map leaves change control at exactly the moment the team is largest. Cross-repo policies restore breadth (protect the default branch of each repository, or current and future branches matching a pattern) but not versioning, and the pattern is case sensitive.
named_tools: GitHub rulesets (require review from Code Owners)
Azure Repos Automatically included reviewers policy
Cross-repo branch policies (Project settings > Repositories > All Repositories > Policies)

silent_failures.failure: A path filter on a branch policy (build validation, status checks, or automatically included reviewers) that does not begin with / or a wildcard matches nothing, so the policy is configured, displayed as On, and enforces nothing. The same applies to a filter consisting only of ! exclusions.
silent_failures.why_invisible: There is no validation error and no warning in the UI or the CLI. The policy list shows the policy as enabled and blocking. Pull requests complete cleanly, which is exactly what a correctly satisfied policy also looks like. The only observable difference between a working required-reviewer policy and a dead one is the absence of a reviewer nobody is looking for.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A deliberate canary pull request per protected path: touch one file under each governed folder and assert the expected reviewer or build appears in the PR Policies section. Automate it as a monthly rehearsal. Independently, enumerate policies with az repos policy list and az repos policy show and assert every filenamePatterns entry starts with / or *, and that no filter is exclusion-only, as a CI check on the settings export.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies (sections 'Use path filters with branch policies' and FAQ 'What happens when a path filter doesn't start with / or a wildcard?'). Verified verbatim August 2026.

silent_failures.failure: Users holding Bypass policies when completing pull requests merge changes that fail required policies, and the pull request still displays the failure.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Microsoft states that the system always evaluates configured policies, but for users who have bypass policy permissions the reported policy status is advisory only, and if such a user approves, the failure status doesn't block completion. The PR shows a red policy, then completes anyway. A reviewer skimming a merged PR sees a failed check next to a successful merge and reads it as a flaky build rather than as an enforcement bypass, because both look identical in the timeline.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: Reconcile, monthly, the set of completed PRs against their final policy evaluation status, and separately audit who holds Bypass policies when completing pull requests and Bypass policies when pushing at project, repo and branch scope. On GitHub the equivalent is auditing ruleset bypass lists. A non-zero count of merged-with-failing-policy PRs is the number to drive to zero, and it must be counted, not estimated.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/repos/git/branch-policies (sections 'Allow policy bypass when needed' and FAQ 'I have bypass policy permissions. Why do I still see policy failures in the pull request status?'). Verified verbatim August 2026.

silent_failures.failure: A custom ARM parameterization entry set to = pins the source (development) factory's value as the parameter default, so any environment whose release does not explicitly override that parameter silently inherits development's value. The sibling failure is a property that is not in the parameterization file at all, such as SnowflakeV2's accountIdentifier, which is hard-coded into the template with no parameter to override.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The ARM deployment succeeds. The linked service, dataset or trigger is structurally valid in the target factory. Pipelines run, activities go green, rows land. The only symptom is that the data came from or went to the wrong system, and where two environments share a schema the row counts and column names look entirely normal. By contrast, - produces a mandatory deployment input and fails loudly, which is precisely why teams under deployment pressure drift towards =.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A post-deployment reconciliation that reads back the deployed linked service and dataset properties from the target factory (Get-AzDataFactoryV2LinkedService, Get-AzDataFactoryV2Dataset) and asserts each accountIdentifier, server, database, url, existingClusterId and folderPath against an expected per-environment manifest, run as a gate before the stage is marked successful. Second derivation: diff the generated ARMTemplateParametersForFactory.json against the release override list and fail if any parameter carries a non-empty defaultValue that no override replaces, and separately grep the generated ARMTemplateForFactory.json for literal development hostnames and account identifiers that never became parameters at all.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-resource-manager-custom-parameters ('= means keep the current value as the default value for the parameter'; 'A definition can't be specific to a resource instance'; default parameterization template, in which accountIdentifier does not appear) and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-automate-azure-pipelines (Override template parameters)

silent_failures.failure: A stale publish branch: adf_publish holds an ARM template older than the collaboration branch, so a green release deploys code that no longer matches main.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The release pipeline is triggered by check-ins to the publish branch, so a publish branch that has quietly stopped receiving updates simply stops triggering, or triggers on old content. Microsoft documents four causes, including deleting a non-Key-Vault linked service in an unmerged feature branch, modifying the factory via the SDK or PowerShell, moving all resources to a new branch and publishing for the first time, and manually uploading a non-AKV linked service or Integration Runtime JSON. In every case the ARM deployment reports success. The gap only surfaces when someone compares deployed behaviour to main by hand. Note also that a second publish branch specified via publish_config.json does not delete the previous one: an abandoned publish branch still wired to an old release trigger is a live deployment source.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: A scheduled freshness check comparing the commit the publish branch was generated from against the head of the collaboration branch, failing if the publish branch is behind, plus an assertion that no release definition has an artifact pointing at a publish branch other than the current one. Under the automated publish flow this failure mode goes away by construction, because the ARM template is generated from the collaboration branch on every build rather than by a human clicking Publish. Second derivation: reconcile resource counts between the exported template and the live factory via Get-AzDataFactoryV2Pipeline, Get-AzDataFactoryV2Dataset and Get-AzDataFactoryV2LinkedService.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/source-control ('Troubleshooting Git integration: Stale publish branch'; 'Azure Data Factory can only have one publish branch at a time... Data Factory doesn't delete the previous publish branch'; 'Data Factory only reads the publish_config.json file when it loads the factory') and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-improvements ('You can continue to use the existing mechanism, which is the adf_publish branch, or you can use the new flow. Both are supported.')

silent_failures.failure: A GitHub Actions federated credential whose subject claim is scoped to a branch rather than an environment grants prod-capable tokens to any workflow run on that branch. The related but louder case: a subject written against the old sub format stops matching on repositories created after July 15, 2026, which now use immutable owner and repository ids.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The branch-scoped case is the silent one. Authentication succeeds, azure/login reports success, the deploy runs. Nothing in the run log distinguishes a token minted from a reviewed environment deployment from one minted by a workflow_dispatch on the same branch by anyone with write access, because the subject claim is the only thing that differed and it is never printed. Environment protection rules only gate secrets and jobs that reference the environment; a branch-scoped federated credential bypasses that gate entirely. The immutable-sub case at least fails loudly at login.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: Enumerate every federated identity credential on the app registrations and managed identities used for deployment and assert each subject uses repo:ORG/REPO:environment:NAME, never :ref:refs/heads/. Then rehearse: run the deploy workflow from a feature branch without the environment and confirm it cannot obtain a token. Mirror the check on the Azure DevOps side by confirming service connections report authorization.scheme WorkloadIdentityFederation rather than ServicePrincipal, using the same serviceendpoint REST query as Microsoft's bulk conversion script.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://docs.github.com/en/actions/reference/security/oidc (subject claim formats; immutable sub repo:OWNER@OWNER-ID/REPO@REPO-ID:ref:refs/heads/BRANCH for repositories created after July 15, 2026), https://docs.github.com/en/actions/how-tos/secure-your-work/security-harden-deployments/oidc-in-azure, https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/devops/pipelines/library/connect-to-azure

silent_failures.failure: PrePostDeploymentScript.Ver2.ps1 stops only modified triggers, so a trigger whose own JSON is unchanged keeps firing throughout an ARM deployment that is rewriting the datasets and pipelines it invokes.
silent_failures.why_invisible: The deployment is green and shorter, which reads as an improvement. The trigger run that fired mid-deployment appears in ADF monitoring as an ordinary successful run, because it usually is successful: dependency ordering guarantees a window in which updated datasets and linked services are already live while the pipelines that were written against them have not landed, so the run executes a coherent-looking but untested combination. The corrupted output is a normal-looking load into a normal-looking target, indistinguishable from a scheduled run five minutes earlier.
silent_failures.what_evidence_would_catch_it: Assert the invariant directly rather than trusting the script's scope: after the predeployment step, query trigger runtime state with Get-AzDataFactoryV2Trigger and fail the stage if any trigger reports Started before the ARM deployment begins. Then reconcile trigger run start times against the deployment's start and end timestamps for every release, and treat any overlap as an incident regardless of run status. An Exclusive lock check on the environment prevents the related case of two releases overlapping on one factory.
silent_failures.doc_reference: https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-sample-script ('Use the PrePostDeploymentScript.Ver2.ps1 if you would like to turn off/ on only the triggers that have been modified') and https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/data-factory/continuous-integration-delivery-automate-azure-pipelines ('Deployment can fail if you try to update active triggers')

silent_failures.failure: An Azure Resource Manager service connection is auto-disabled after 100 days of non-use, breaking a low-frequency promotion path (annual DR rehearsal, quarterly prod-only release, the rollback pipeline) at exactly the moment it is needed.
silent_failures.why_invisible: Not silent at run time, it fails loudly. It is silent in planning: nothing surfaces the countdown, and the connections most at risk are precisely the ones nobody exercises, so the failure is discovered inside an incident window rather than during normal work. Microsoft's wording is 'Azure Pipelines is starting to automatically disable service connections that haven't been used for 100 days', and re-enabling requires a service connection administrator or Project Administrator, which adds a permissions hop to an outage.

Supplement with a periodic REST enumeration of service connections and their last-used date, alerting past 70 days, and pair it with the seven-day revert window on any recent workload identity federation conversion so a botched conversion is not discovered on day eight.
